definition: To pull someone or something in a particular direction.
example: She drew the chair closer to the table.
distinctions: The verb describes pulling or moving the object, not making its picture. Draw has the forms draw–drew–drawn.

originalSense.definition: To pull (someone or something) in a particular direction or manner.

distinctionTask.prompt: The usual past and past participle of draw are _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Draw is irregular: draw–drew–drawn.

definition: To move a part of the body in a particular direction.
example: He drew his hand back from the hot cup.
distinctions: The body part moves in the specified direction. This is different from drawing a picture of it.

originalSense.definition: To move (a body part) in a particular direction.

definition: To pull something so that it becomes tighter.
example: She drew the belt tight around the bundle.
distinctions: Tight describes the resulting condition; this use concerns tension, rather than making a drawing.
usage: Transitive verb; often followed by tight.

originalSense.definition: Often followed by tight: to pull (something, such as a belt or string) so that it tightens or wraps around something more closely.

distinctionTask.prompt: “Draw the string tight” means pull it until it becomes _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Tight specifies the resulting physical condition.

definition: To drag something, especially along the ground.
example: The horse drew the cart along the lane.
distinctions: This pulling use moves a load. It does not describe drawing an illustration of the cart.

originalSense.definition: To drag (something), especially along the ground.

definition: To pull curtains or blinds open or closed.
example: She drew the curtains closed before turning on the lamp.
distinctions: Draw the curtains can mean open or close them, depending on context. State open or closed when the direction would otherwise be unclear.

originalSense.definition: To pull (blinds, a curtain, etc.) open or closed.

distinctionTask.prompt: “Draw the curtains” _____ opening rather than closing them.
distinctionTask.explanation: The direction depends on context; open or closed makes it explicit.

definition: To move a bolt or latch into or out of its locking position.
example: In a door description, drawing the bolt can refer to moving it to lock or unlock, as the construction and context specify.
distinctions: The unqualified expression is context-dependent. Draw back the bolt normally clarifies withdrawal rather than insertion.

originalSense.definition: To pull out (a bolt or latch) to unlock a door, gate, etc.; also, to push in (a bolt or latch) to lock a door, gate, etc.

definition: To take someone to one side for a private conversation.
example: The manager drew me aside after the meeting.
distinctions: Aside supplies the private or separate direction. It does not mean sketching the person.
usage: Transitive verb; usually with aside or to one side.

originalSense.definition: Chiefly followed by aside or to one side: to move (someone) away from a group of people in order to speak to them privately.

distinctionTask.prompt: To speak privately, the manager drew her _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Draw someone aside moves them away from the group for a separate exchange.

definition: To move one’s own body into a particular posture.
example: She drew herself up before answering.
distinctions: The reflexive object is the person adopting the posture. Draw someone else up is not the same reflexive construction.

originalSense.definition: To assume a specific attitude or position, either by pulling in or stretching out one's body or limbs.

definition: To contract or distort a body part or facial feature.
example: In a description of discomfort, pain may draw the features into a strained expression.
distinctions: This source use describes contraction or distortion, not necessarily deliberate facial movement or picture-making.

originalSense.definition: To cause (a body part) to contract or shrink; also, to pull (the mouth, the face or features, etc.) out of shape from emotion, etc.; to distort.

definition: To cause someone or something to move between places or conditions.
example: In an archaic passage, draw can mean cause a person or thing to pass into another place or condition.
collocations: draw from one state to another
distinctions: This broad historical causative use is distinct from the specific modern phrasal verbs that may look similar.

originalSense.definition: To cause (someone or something) to go from one place to another, or from one condition to another.

definition: To construct a wall, canal or similar feature from one position to another.
example: In an older construction account, drawing a wall can mean building it along a line.
distinctions: The historical construction sense is not the same as making a plan or sketch of the wall.

originalSense.definition: To construct (a canal, wall, etc.) from one point to another.

definition: To give the cue ball backspin so that it can move back after contacting another ball.
example: In billiards, drawing the cue ball refers to applying backspin for a return movement after contact.
distinctions: The outcome depends on the actual shot and conditions. This is separate from drawing a contest or tracing a line on the table.

originalSense.definition: To strike (the cue ball) below the centre so as to give it a backward rotation which causes it to move backwards on striking another ball.

definition: To make a bowl travel along a curve towards a chosen position.
example: In bowls terminology, drawing a bowl concerns placing it along a curved path.
distinctions: The sport uses a biased bowl; this movement sense is distinct from a drawn match result.

originalSense.definition: To cause (a bowl) to move in a curve to a certain place.

definition: To deflect a cricket ball towards the leg side with the bat, in an archaic use.
example: The source records draw for certain older cricket strokes directing the ball towards the leg side.
distinctions: This is historical stroke terminology, separate from a cricket match ending in a draw.

originalSense.definition: Of a batter: to hit (a ball) from the off side to the leg side, especially with an inclined bat; also, to hit (a short-length ball directed at the leg stump) with an inclined bat so as to deflect the ball between the legs and the wicket.

definition: To play a curling shot intended to land in the house.
example: She drew the stone into the house.
distinctions: The house is curling’s circular target area. A draw is intended for placement rather than a takeout, and can miss its intended position.

originalSense.definition: To play (a shot or a stone) that lands in the house (circular target).

definition: To hit a controlled curving golf shot, right to left for a right-handed player and reversed for a left-handed player.
example: The right-handed player drew the ball around the obstacle.
distinctions: The curve is described from behind the player facing the target. The preserved gloss mentions club-toe contact; a modern draw is not defined by universally requiring that contact point.

originalSense.definition: To hit (the ball) with the toe of the club so that it is deflected toward the left (or, for a left-handed player, toward the right, originally in an uncontrolled and now a controlled manner.

definition: Of a vessel, to require a stated depth of water to float.
example: The vessel draws three metres.
distinctions: The stated draught is the vertical distance from the waterline to the lowest relevant part of the vessel. It is not the total water depth or the clearance beneath the keel.

originalSense.definition: Of a vessel: to require (a certain depth of water) to float in.

distinctionTask.prompt: A vessel’s stated draught is _____ its under-keel clearance.
distinctionTask.explanation: Draught concerns the vessel below the waterline; clearance concerns the remaining space below the keel.

definition: To drag a person as a historical punishment or to a place of execution.
example: In one historical punishment sense, drawn refers to a captive being dragged to execution.
distinctions: This reading is distinct from tearing the body apart and from the disembowelling sense in another branch of draw. Historical wording requires context.

originalSense.definition: To drag (someone) by tying behind a horse or on a frame as a form of punishment or torture, or to bring to a place of execution.

definition: To tear a person’s body apart as a historical punishment.

originalSense.definition: To kill someone as a form of punishment or torture by tearing apart (their body) by tying their limbs to horses which run in different directions; also, to tear (the limbs) from someone's body in this manner.

definition: To pull back an arrow or bowstring in preparation for a shot.
example: The archer drew the bow and waited for the signal.
distinctions: Drawing prepares the bow; releasing is a separate action. The verb does not mean producing an illustration of the bow.

originalSense.definition: To pull back (an arrow or bowstring) in preparation for shooting the arrow; also, to cause (a bow) to bend by pulling back the bowstring.

definition: To apply an arithmetic operation to a number, in a specialised use.
example: The source records draw as an arithmetic verb for subjecting a number to an operation.
distinctions: The surrounding text must identify the operation. The verb alone does not universally mean subtraction or drawing a number at random.

originalSense.definition: To subject (a number) to an arithmetic operation.

definition: To haul in or tow a fishing net.
example: In a fishing account, drawing a net can mean hauling it in or dragging it alongside a boat.
distinctions: This use concerns moving the net. It is distinct from drawing a picture and from fishing a whole stretch of water by dragging a net.

originalSense.definition: to haul in (a fishing net) which has been cast; also, to drag (a fishing net) alongside a boat.

definition: To hoist a sail, in an archaic nautical use.
example: In the recorded older nautical use, drawing a sail means hoisting it.
distinctions: This is separate from a sail drawing when it fills with wind. Modern hoist is clearer when raising the sail is intended.

originalSense.definition: To hoist (a sail).

definition: To carry a load in a vehicle; to haul or cart it.

distinctions: This regional carrying sense is separate from sketching a load or withdrawing money.

originalSense.definition: To carry (a load) in a vehicle; to cart, to haul.

definition: To sew together or mend torn fabric, in an obsolete use.
example: In an older textile passage, drawing a tear can refer to sewing its edges together.
distinctions: This historical sewing use is different from making a drawn representation of the damage.

originalSense.definition: To sew together (the edges of a tear); also, to mend (a hole or tear) in fabric.

definition: To use a draught animal to pull a vehicle or plough, in an obsolete use.
example: The source records an obsolete object-taking use of draw for employing a draught animal.
distinctions: Here the historical verb takes the animal as its object, unlike the modern construction the horse draws the cart.

originalSense.definition: To use (a draught animal) to pull a plough or vehicle.

definition: To attribute or ascribe something to a person or thing.
example: In an obsolete figurative passage, draw can mean ascribe a quality or action to someone.
distinctions: This historical attribution use is distinct from drawing information from a source in ordinary modern writing.

originalSense.definition: To attribute (something) to a person or thing; to ascribe.

definition: To transform or convert something into something else.
example: The source records draw as an obsolete figurative verb for conversion or transformation.
distinctions: Modern change or transform is clearer for this intended meaning; the historical use does not necessarily involve physical pulling.

originalSense.definition: To change (something) into another thing; to convert, to transform.

definition: To recast or translate a text into another style or language.
example: In an older literary description, a work drawn into verse has been recast in verse.
distinctions: This is textual conversion, rather than adding pictures or drawing up a new document.

originalSense.definition: To convert (a passage) from one literary style to another (for example, from prose to verse); or to translate (a text) from one language to another.

definition: To direct one’s heart or thoughts towards something.
example: In an obsolete figurative use, draw can mean direct a person’s thoughts or heart towards an object.
distinctions: This recorded inward-direction sense is separate from attracting another person’s attention in modern usage.

originalSense.definition: To direct (one's heart, thoughts, etc.) in a certain way or towards someone or something.

definition: To summon strength or courage, or produce a quality in oneself, in an obsolete use.
example: The source records an older draw use for summoning courage or bringing a quality into oneself.

originalSense.definition: To give (courage, strength, etc.) to oneself; to summon up; also, to produce (evil, wickedness, etc.) in oneself.

definition: To give words a particular, especially distorted, interpretation.

distinctions: This is a historical interpretation use, not a claim that every inference drawn from words misrepresents them.

originalSense.definition: To give (words) a certain meaning, especially one which is distorted; to distort, to misrepresent.

definition: To pass food through a strainer, in an obsolete cooking use.

originalSense.definition: Followed by through: to pass (food) through a strainer.

originalSense.definition: To mix (an ingredient) with another ingredient or ingredients to form a liquid or paste; to mix (ingredients) together to form a liquid or paste.

definition: Of a bowl, to travel in a curve towards a position.

originalSense.definition: Of a bowl: to move in a curve to a certain place.

definition: To make a curling shot intended to finish in the house.
example: With her final stone, she drew to the centre of the house.
distinctions: The verb is used without a direct object here. A draw remains a placement attempt, rather than a guaranteed result or a takeout.

originalSense.definition: To make a shot that lands in the house.

definition: Of a vessel, to have a draught described as deep or shallow.
example: In nautical description, a vessel that draws deep requires relatively deep water to float.
distinctions: This describes the vessel’s draught. It is separate from the depth of the entire waterway and from the vessel moving downward.

originalSense.definition: Followed by an adverb, such as deep or shallow: of a vessel: to require a depth of water of a certain characteristic to float in.

definition: Of a draught animal, to pull or have pulling power.
example: In an older farming account, an animal that draws well pulls effectively.
distinctions: The animal is the subject of this historical intransitive use, not the object in the separate obsolete construction employing an animal.

originalSense.definition: Especially of a draught animal: to pull something, such as a plough or vehicle, along; to have force to move something by pulling.

definition: Of a plough or vehicle, to be pulled in a specified manner.
example: In an older description, a plough that draws easily is easy to pull.
distinctions: The plough or vehicle is what is moved. The verb does not describe making an illustration of it.

originalSense.definition: Of a plough or vehicle: to be pulled along in a specified manner.

definition: To contract or shrink, in an archaic use.
example: The source records intransitive draw for becoming contracted or smaller.
distinctions: This older shrinkage use differs from stretching something longer and from drawing in air.

originalSense.definition: To become contracted; to shrink.

definition: To pull back a bowstring or arrow in preparation for shooting.
example: At the signal, the archers drew and held.
distinctions: No direct object is expressed in this use. Drawing is the preparation, rather than the release of the arrow.

originalSense.definition: To pull back an arrow or bowstring in preparation for shooting the arrow; also, to cause a bow to bend by pulling back the bowstring.

definition: To cooperate or get on well, in an archaic Scottish use.
example: In the recorded older Scottish use, people who draw work together towards a common aim or get on with each other.
distinctions: This regional historical reading is separate from pulling an object together and from a match ending without a winner.

originalSense.definition: To work together towards a common aim; to cooperate, to pull together; also, to have a good relationship with; to get on with.

definition: To be dragged along, in an obsolete use.
example: In the obsolete intransitive reading, a thing that draws is being dragged along.
distinctions: This passive-like historical meaning is distinct from an animal actively pulling a load.

originalSense.definition: To be dragged along; to drag.

definition: To tug or pull at something, in an obsolete intransitive use.
example: The source records intransitive draw for pulling or tugging at something.
distinctions: The object of pulling is not a direct object in this recorded construction. Ordinary pull or tug is clearer in modern general use.

originalSense.definition: To pull at something; to tug.

definition: To attract attention or direct someone’s thoughts towards something.
example: The bright sign drew our attention to the entrance.
distinctions: Draw attention to directs notice towards a subject. It need not involve pulling someone physically or moving them to the location.

originalSense.definition: To induce (the attention, the eyes or mind, etc.) to be directed at or focused on something.

distinctionTask.prompt: The sign drew our attention _____ the entrance.
distinctionTask.explanation: Draw attention to identifies the object of notice.

definition: To attract someone to a place or course of action.
example: The exhibition drew visitors from nearby towns.
distinctions: The verb brings people or their interest towards something, or away from another condition. It is distinct from drawing a picture of those people.

originalSense.definition: To attract or cause (someone) to come to a particular place or to take a particular course of action; also, to cause (someone) to turn away from a particular condition or course of action.

distinctionTask.prompt: An exhibition that draws visitors _____ them.
distinctionTask.explanation: The attendance context selects attraction.

definition: To attract material through a physical force such as gravity or magnetism.
example: The magnet drew the iron filings towards it.
distinctions: The mechanism depends on the force and material. Not every metal is attracted in the same way by an ordinary magnet.

originalSense.definition: To attract (something) by means of a physical force, especially gravity or magnetism.

definition: To provoke or elicit a reaction from someone.
example: The proposal drew criticism from local residents.
distinctions: The response is elicited rather than physically pulled. Draw a conclusion instead describes an inference from information.

originalSense.definition: To attract or provoke (a particular reaction or response) from someone.

distinctionTask.prompt: A proposal that draws criticism _____ a response.
distinctionTask.explanation: The verb describes provoking the response.

definition: To bring about an event or consequence.
example: In the source’s broader causative use, draw can mean bring about a consequence, rather than pull a physical object.
distinctions: This broad recorded use overlaps more specific reaction and misfortune constructions. The exact object and surrounding text determine the intended consequence.

originalSense.definition: To cause (something) to occur as a consequence; to bring about.

definition: To bring trouble or misfortune upon oneself.
example: He drew trouble on himself by ignoring the agreement.
distinctions: On or upon identifies who receives the consequence. Drawing trouble on oneself is different from sketching a troublesome scene.
usage: Transitive causative verb; with on or upon.

originalSense.definition: Followed by on or upon: to bring (disaster or misfortune) on oneself.

definition: To receive a particular prison sentence.
example: The report said that he drew a six-month prison sentence.
distinctions: This use means receive a sentence, not pronounce it or determine a universal punishment for an offence.

originalSense.definition: To receive (a particular prison sentence).

definition: To take air or smoke into the lungs.
example: She drew a deep breath before speaking.
distinctions: The breath is taken in; this is distinct from producing a picture of breathing or physically drawing another person closer.

originalSense.definition: To take (air, smoke, etc.) into the lungs; to breathe in, to inhale.

distinctionTask.prompt: “She drew a deep breath” describes _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The breath is taken into the lungs.

definition: To cause air to enter a duct, room or other space.
example: The fan draws air into the duct.
distinctions: This verb describes bulk airflow into a space. It is different from sound propagating as a disturbance through the air.

originalSense.definition: To cause (air) to be sucked into a duct, a room, etc.

distinctionTask.prompt: A fan that draws air into a duct causes air to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This is physical airflow.

definition: To take a deep pull on a smoking implement, in an archaic transitive use.
example: The source records an older object-taking use of draw for taking a deep pull on a pipe or similar smoking implement.
distinctions: This historical transitive construction is separate from the current construction draw on a pipe.

originalSense.definition: To drag or suck deeply on (a cigarette, pipe, or other smoking implement).

definition: To attract gunfire, intentionally or unintentionally.
example: The decoy drew fire away from the convoy.
distinctions: The literal military sense concerns incoming gunfire. Figurative draw fire can instead mean attract criticism; context distinguishes them.

originalSense.definition: To attract or provoke gunfire, either intentionally or unintentionally.

definition: To attract people or act as an inducement, without a stated direct object.
example: The show still draws, even after many years.
distinctions: The audience or people attracted are understood rather than named as a direct object. This is separate from making a drawing.

originalSense.definition: To attract or influence a person or group of people; to be an inducement or enticement.

definition: To take a drink, especially of an alcoholic beverage.
example: The source records intransitive draw for taking a drink or swig.
distinctions: This source-bound drinking use is distinct from drawing a beverage from a keg, which describes taking it out of the container.

originalSense.definition: To take a drink of a beverage, especially an alcoholic one; to swig.

definition: Of a flue or similar passage, to permit airflow associated with combustion.
example: The inspector reported that the chimney was drawing well.
distinctions: The verb describes airflow through the passage, not a picture of it. A report about draw alone does not describe every aspect of the appliance’s condition.

originalSense.definition: Of a duct, smoking implement, etc.: to allow air to be passed through it in order that combustion can occur.

definition: To take a pull on a cigarette, pipe or similar smoking implement.
example: In the construction draw on a pipe, draw refers to taking a pull on the smoking implement.
distinctions: The preposition introduces the implement; this is separate from draw on a source meaning use it for support or information.
usage: Intransitive smoking-related reading; with at or on.

originalSense.definition: Followed by at or on: to drag or suck deeply on a cigarette, pipe, or other smoking implement.

definition: Of people, to gather together around a person or place.
example: The children drew around the guide to listen.
distinctions: Around or about identifies the gathering place. The group comes together; no one needs to be making a picture.

originalSense.definition: Chiefly followed by about or around: of a group of people: to come together; to assemble, to congregate, to gather.

definition: To lengthen or stretch something.
example: The metal was drawn into a long, thin strip.
distinctions: This is physical elongation. Drawing out a conversation instead extends its duration.

originalSense.definition: To make (something) larger or longer; to elongate, to stretch.

definition: To flatten metal, commonly by hammering, in the construction draw out.
example: In the recorded metalworking use, draw out can describe flattening a piece of metal, often by hammering.
distinctions: This source use concerns shaping metal. It is distinct from drawing out a reply or withdrawing money.

originalSense.definition: Followed by out: to flatten (a piece of metal), usually by hammering.

definition: To form or reduce wire by pulling metal through a die or aperture.
example: The manufacturer draws wire through a series of dies.
distinctions: The metal passes through an opening and changes cross-section. Wire drawing is a manufacturing process, not a drawn diagram of a wire.

originalSense.definition: To make (wire) by pulling a rod or other piece of metal through one or more apertures; also, to stretch (a rod or other piece of metal) into a wire.

distinctionTask.prompt: Wire drawing shapes metal by pulling it through a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The named manufacturing process changes the metal’s cross-section.

definition: To straighten straw for thatching by pulling it through the hands.
example: In thatching terminology, drawing straw means preparing it into a straight, aligned condition.
distinctions: This preparatory sense is distinct from drawing straws at random to decide who does something.

originalSense.definition: To make (straw straight for thatching by pulling it through the hands.

definition: To amount to a specified quantity or sum.
example: The source records an obsolete object-taking use of draw meaning amount to a quantity or sum.
distinctions: This historical numerical use is not a command to select a random number or withdraw that sum.

originalSense.definition: To amount to (a certain quantity or sum).

definition: To prolong the duration of something, in an obsolete bare-verb use.
example: The source marks this bare prolonging use obsolete; modern draw out can still mean prolong a discussion or event.
distinctions: Do not label the modern phrasal verb draw out obsolete merely because this separately recorded bare use is obsolete.
usage: Obsolete transitive reading; compare current draw out.

originalSense.definition: To extend the duration of (something); to prolong.

definition: To stretch a person on a rack as a historical punishment.
example: In a historical punishment account, draw can denote forced stretching on a rack.
distinctions: This is a distinct historical reading from dragging to execution or disembowelling.

originalSense.definition: To stretch (someone) on a rack as a form of punishment or torture.

definition: To become longer or stretched.
example: In this intransitive elongation use, the subject itself is stretched or lengthened.
distinctions: This is the non-object-taking counterpart of drawing material longer. It does not mean that the material makes a picture.

originalSense.definition: To be made larger or longer; to be elongated or stretched.

definition: To straighten thatching straw by pulling it through the hands, without a stated direct object.
example: The source also records an intransitive thatching use of draw for preparing straw straight.
distinctions: The activity is understood from the thatching context; this is separate from random selection by drawing straws.

originalSense.definition: To make straw straight for thatching by pulling it through the hands.

definition: Of a sail, to fill with wind and become taut.
example: The sail began to draw as the breeze strengthened.
distinctions: A drawing sail is filling and working in the wind. This differs from the archaic object-taking use draw a sail meaning hoist it.

originalSense.definition: Of a sail: to fill with wind and become taut.

definition: To amount to a quantity or sum, without a direct object.
example: The source separately records an obsolete intransitive amounting use of draw.
distinctions: This is the intransitive counterpart of the obsolete quantity use, rather than a modern drawing or withdrawal instruction.

originalSense.definition: To amount to a certain quantity or sum.

definition: To extend or spread over an area or through space.
example: In an obsolete spatial use, draw can mean spread or stretch over an area.
distinctions: This historical extension sense is different from moving steadily in a direction in a modern phrasal construction.

originalSense.definition: To extend in area or space; to spread, to stretch.

definition: To pull something out of a place or container.
example: She drew a letter from the envelope.
distinctions: This is physical extraction. It need not involve a random selection or drawing a conclusion.

originalSense.definition: To pull (something) out; to extract, to remove.

distinctionTask.prompt: “She drew a letter from the envelope” describes _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: From the envelope selects physical extraction.

definition: To extract a tooth.
example: In a dental narrative, to draw a tooth means to extract it.
distinctions: This formal or older dental expression is separate from drawing a picture of a tooth. It names the action rather than explaining a procedure.

originalSense.definition: To extract (a tooth); to pull.

definition: To extract juice, oil or another fluid from something.
example: The salt drew moisture out of the sliced vegetables.
distinctions: The verb names extraction; the mechanism depends on the materials and process. It does not universally imply suction or one particular physical mechanism.

originalSense.definition: To extract (juice, oil, or some other fluid) from something by osmosis, pressure, or another process.

definition: To extract a small fluid sample, especially blood.
example: The nurse drew a blood sample for the test.
distinctions: This sample-taking use is distinct from a blow drawing blood and from drawing an anatomical picture. The vocabulary does not specify one sampling method.

originalSense.definition: To extract (a small amount of liquid, especially blood) by puncturing a surface, or by using a pipette, syringe, or other suction device.

distinctionTask.prompt: A nurse who draws a blood sample _____ it for testing.
distinctionTask.explanation: Draw a sample means obtain a specimen.

definition: To let tea infuse in water.
example: The source records an object-taking use of draw for allowing tea to infuse.
distinctions: This brewing sense is separate from pouring tea from a pot. Let the tea draw is the related intransitive construction.

originalSense.definition: To leave (tea) temporarily in water to allow the flavour to increase; to infuse, to steep.

definition: To pull a weapon from its holder or sheath.
example: The actor drew a sword during the scene.
distinctions: The object is taken out, rather than depicted in a picture. The context may be a staged performance rather than a real conflict.

originalSense.definition: To pull out (a firearm, sword, or other weapon) from a holster, sheath, etc.; to unsheathe.

definition: To take a beverage from a cask or keg using a pump or tap.
example: In a serving context, drawing a beverage takes it from a cask or keg.
distinctions: This use describes serving or extraction, not necessarily drinking the beverage.

originalSense.definition: To take (a beverage) from a cask or keg using a pump or tap; to tap.

definition: To take water from a well or other source.
example: They drew water from the well.
distinctions: Water is obtained from the source, for example by lifting or pumping. The verb does not identify one universal mechanism.

originalSense.definition: To take up (water) from a well or other source, especially by lifting in a container or pumping.

distinctionTask.prompt: To draw water from a well is to _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: The source context selects water extraction.

definition: To absorb liquid or nutrients, especially through a plant’s roots.
example: The roots draw water from the soil.
distinctions: This is uptake from the surroundings, not making a picture of the roots. Different substances and conditions involve different uptake processes.

originalSense.definition: To soak up (a liquid, etc.); to absorb; specifically, of an organism (especially a plant) or one of its parts: to take in (nutrients, water, etc.).

definition: Of a channel or drain, to carry water away.
example: The drain draws water away from the courtyard.
distinctions: The drainage context concerns removal of water, rather than drinking, picture-making or a random selection.

originalSense.definition: Of a channel, drain, etc.: to carry (water) away.

definition: To disembowel a person, in a historical punishment use.
example: In the recorded execution terminology, drawn can refer to disembowelling, particularly in accounts of hanging, drawing and quartering.
distinctions: Other branches of draw separately record dragging to execution and tearing apart. Do not infer one reading solely from the spelling drawn.

originalSense.definition: Chiefly in draw and quarter and hang, draw and quarter: to disembowel (someone), especially after hanging as a punishment for high treason.

definition: To remove an animal’s internal organs before cooking.
example: In older food-preparation terminology, drawing a bird means removing its internal organs.
distinctions: This culinary sense is separate from attracting birds and from drawing their pictures.

originalSense.definition: To remove the viscera from (an animal, especially a bird) before cooking.

definition: To bring bodily material towards the surface for removal, in historical medicine.
example: The source records draw in an older medical theory of attracting humours or pus towards the body’s surface.
distinctions: This reading reflects historical medical terminology and theory. It should not be read as a general modern explanation of how wounds are treated.

originalSense.definition: To attract (humours, pus, etc.), chiefly by bringing to the surface of the body, so it can be dispersed or removed; also, to treat (a wound) in this way.

definition: To raise coal or ore from an underground mine to the surface.
example: In mining terminology, drawing ore brings it from underground to the surface.
distinctions: This is extraction or hoisting, not a geological sketch or a lottery selection.

originalSense.definition: To raise (coal or ore) from an underground mine to the surface.

definition: To select one or more items from a collection by a random or chance procedure.
example: Each participant drew one numbered ticket from the bag.
distinctions: A draw selects an item or person. The word alone does not guarantee uniform chances or a fair procedure.

originalSense.definition: To select (one or more things) at random from a collection of similar things to decide which of a group of people will receive something such as a prize, or undergo something such as an assignment; also, to select (someone) by this process; to win (a prize) in a lottery or lucky draw.

distinctionTask.prompt: A lottery draw _____ guarantee equal chances without regard to procedure.
distinctionTask.explanation: The actual selection procedure determines the probabilities.

definition: To conduct a lottery selection or select its winning numbers or tickets.
example: The winning numbers will be drawn at noon.
distinctions: This use determines the lottery result. It is separate from describing a match with no winner.

originalSense.definition: To conduct, or select the winning numbers, tickets, etc., for, (a lottery).

definition: To empty the contents of a kiln, oven or similar enclosure.
example: In kiln terminology, drawing the kiln means removing its contents.
distinctions: The kiln or oven is the object of this emptying use, unlike draw a kiln meaning sketch its appearance.

originalSense.definition: To remove the contents of (something, especially a kiln or oven); to empty.

definition: To fill a bathtub with water for a bath.
example: She drew a bath for the child.
distinctions: Draw a bath means prepare its water, rather than make a picture of the bathtub.

originalSense.definition: To fill a bathtub with (water for a bath); to run (a bath).

distinctionTask.prompt: To draw a bath is to _____ it with water.
distinctionTask.explanation: The household expression means prepare the bathwater.

definition: To withdraw something, such as a bet or a horse from a race.
example: The source records archaic draw for withdrawing a wager or withdrawing a horse from a race.
collocations: draw a horse from a race (archaic)
distinctions: Withdraw is clearer in ordinary modern writing. This older use is separate from allocating the horse’s starting draw.

originalSense.definition: To withdraw (something); specifically , to withdraw (a bet or wager); also , to withdraw (a horse) from a race.

definition: Of plants or roots, to deplete soil of nutrients.
example: In the recorded regional agricultural sense, drawing soil emphasises depletion of its nutrients.
distinctions: This source use emphasises the effect on the soil, rather than merely naming neutral absorption by the plant. It does not assert that every uptake event leaves soil depleted.

originalSense.definition: Of a plant or its roots: to deplete (soil) of nutrients.

definition: To separate selected sheep from a flock for a particular purpose.
example: The farmer drew the lambs from the flock for sale.
distinctions: This agricultural use selects and separates animals. It is distinct from sketching the flock or necessarily selecting animals at random.

originalSense.definition: To separate (sheep) from a flock for a particular purpose, such as breeding or selling.

definition: To take or be dealt a playing card from a deck.
example: He drew a card from the top of the deck.
distinctions: Drawing obtains a card. Discarding removes one from a hand, and the game’s rules determine whether and how either action is available.

originalSense.definition: To be dealt or to take (a playing card) from the deck; also, to have (a particular hand) as a result of this.

distinctionTask.prompt: In a card game, drawing a card is _____ discarding one.
distinctionTask.explanation: Drawing obtains a card; discarding removes one from the hand.

definition: To fish an area of water by dragging a net along or through it.
example: In the source’s fishing use, drawing a stretch of water means working it with a dragged net.
collocations: draw a shore with a net
distinctions: Here the water area is the object, rather than the net itself in draw in the net.

originalSense.definition: To fish by dragging a fishing net along (a shore) or in (a body of water).

definition: To search a wood or covert for game.
example: In hunting terminology, drawing a covert means searching it for quarry.
distinctions: The place is searched, not sketched. This meaning is separate from drawing a weapon.

originalSense.definition: To search (a covert, a wood, etc.) for game or a quarry.

definition: To finish a game or match with neither side winning.
example: The two teams drew the league match one–one.
distinctions: The sport’s rules determine the result. A cricket draw can differ from both an equal score and a tie.

originalSense.definition: To end (a game or match) with neither side winning, that is, in a draw.

definition: To finish a timed cricket match without a win or tie because the required innings are not completed.
example: A two-innings cricket match can be drawn when time ends without a winning result, even if the teams’ totals are unequal.
distinctions: A cricket draw is different from a tie. The usual tie requires completed innings and equal scores; a draw need not have equal totals.

originalSense.definition: In a match scheduled to last for a certain period of time: to end (a match) with neither side winning because the team batting last has not completed its innings when the playing time concludes.

definition: To separate lengths of machine-made lace by removing connecting threads.
example: In historical lace manufacture, drawing separates sections joined during production.
distinctions: This industrial use is different from pulling on a lace that fastens clothing.

originalSense.definition: To separate (a length of lace made by machine) into sections by removing the threads connecting the sections.

definition: To milk a cow, in a northern Scottish use.
example: The source records draw a cow as a northern Scottish expression meaning milk the cow.
distinctions: This regional verb does not mean sketching the animal. Milk is the ordinary general English verb.

originalSense.definition: To take milk from (a cow); to milk.

definition: To separate clover or trefoil seeds from their husks.
example: The source records an obsolete agricultural use of draw for separating clover or trefoil seeds from husks.
distinctions: This specific historical processing use differs from sowing seeds or selecting them at random.

originalSense.definition: To separate (seeds) from the husks of clover or trefoil; also, to separate seeds from the husks of (clover or trefoil).

definition: To take a wicket, in a rare obsolete cricket use.
example: The source records a rare obsolete cricket use of draw meaning take a wicket.
distinctions: This is not the current match-result sense of drawing a cricket match.

originalSense.definition: To take (a wicket).

definition: To remove a hawk from its mew after moulting.
example: In the recorded falconry use, drawing a hawk removes it from its mew after it has moulted.
collocations: draw a hawk from the mew
distinctions: The hawk is the object of this specialised historical use. It is distinct from attracting a wild bird.

originalSense.definition: To remove (a hawk) from a mew after it has moulted.

definition: To steal, particularly by pickpocketing, in historical thieves’ slang.
example: The source records draw in obsolete thieves’ cant for stealing from a person or place.
distinctions: This is historical slang for theft, not ordinary drawing from one’s own bank account.

originalSense.definition: To steal (something) from a person, especially by picking a pocket; also to pick the pocket of (someone); to steal from (a place).

definition: To consume or take electrical power.
example: The heater draws two kilowatts while running.
distinctions: Kilowatts measure power; kilowatt-hours measure energy. At a constant 2 kW for one hour, the energy is 2 kWh. The example is not a measured appliance specification.

originalSense.definition: To consume (power).

distinctionTask.prompt: At a constant draw of 2 kW for one hour, energy used is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Power multiplied by duration gives energy; kW and kWh are different quantities.

definition: To obtain or elicit something.
example: The source uses this broad entry to introduce obtaining information, eliciting a response, inferring a conclusion and receiving money.
distinctions: Choose the specific child meaning for the actual context; obtaining a conclusion differs from physically withdrawing money.
usage: Broad lexical umbrella; specific children listed separately.

originalSense.definition: To obtain, elicit.

definition: To derive material or information from a source.
example: The report draws its evidence from interviews.
distinctions: From identifies the origin of the material. The quality of a source is a separate question from whether the report uses it.

originalSense.definition: To take (something) from a particular source, especially of information; to derive.

distinctionTask.prompt: “The report draws evidence from interviews” identifies the evidence’s _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: From identifies origin without independently proving quality.

definition: To elicit a response or statement from someone.
example: The question drew an honest answer from her.
distinctions: The response is brought forth, not necessarily deduced as a conclusion or quoted from a document.

originalSense.definition: To call forth (something) from a person, to elicit.

definition: To infer or reach a conclusion from information.
example: We drew a cautious conclusion from the results.
distinctions: Drawing a conclusion describes making an inference. Its justification depends on the evidence and reasoning; the verb alone does not make it proven.

originalSense.definition: To deduce or infer (a conclusion); to make (a deduction).

distinctionTask.prompt: To draw a conclusion is to make an _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A conclusion’s strength depends on its supporting evidence and reasoning.

definition: To receive pay or withdraw money from an account.
example: She draws a salary from the college.
distinctions: Receiving a salary and withdrawing money are related money-obtaining uses, but salary receipt does not require physically taking cash from a bank.

originalSense.definition: To receive (a salary); to withdraw (money) from a bank etc.

distinctionTask.prompt: A person who draws a salary _____ pay.
distinctionTask.explanation: The financial context selects receipt of pay.

definition: To induce someone to speak or provide information on a subject.
example: She declined to be drawn on the proposed merger.
distinctions: The passive phrase means be induced to discuss the topic. Draw someone out is a related way to encourage them to speak more freely.

originalSense.definition: To elicit information from (someone); to induce (a person) to speak on some subject. (Now frequently in passive.)

distinctionTask.prompt: Someone who declines to be drawn on a topic refuses to be induced to _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: This passive construction concerns providing comments or information.

definition: To take a weapon from its holder, without a stated direct object.
example: In the duel scene, both actors drew.
distinctions: The weapon is understood from context rather than stated as a direct object. This is distinct from making a picture or drawing a card.

originalSense.definition: To pull out a firearm, sword, or other weapon from a holster, sheath, etc.

definition: To take water from a well or source, without a stated direct object.
example: In a well-side account, draw can stand without an object when taking water is understood.
distinctions: The unstated thing obtained is water. This is separate from an audience attraction that draws well.

originalSense.definition: To take up water from a well or other source, especially by lifting it in a container or pumping it.

definition: To make a chance selection without stating the selected item as a direct object.
example: We mixed the numbered tickets, and then it was my turn to draw.
distinctions: The tickets or other items are understood from context. The selection method determines the chances; draw alone does not guarantee fairness.

originalSense.definition: To select one or more things at random from a collection of similar things to decide which of a group of people will receive or undergo something.

definition: Of tea, to infuse; of a pot, to allow tea to infuse.
example: Let the tea draw before you pour it.
distinctions: Tea drawing concerns infusion, not pouring it out or making a picture. The desired time depends on the tea and preparation.

originalSense.definition: To leave tea temporarily in water to allow the flavour to increase; to infuse, to steep; also, of a teapot: to cause tea to infuse.

distinctionTask.prompt: Tea that is drawing is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The brewing use concerns contact with water and developing flavour.

definition: Of a bath, to be filled with water.
example: The source records a bath drawing as a bath being filled with water.
distinctions: The bath is the subject of this recorded use, unlike someone drawing a bath in the transitive construction.

originalSense.definition: Of a bathtub: to be filled with water for a bath; to be run.

definition: Of a channel or drain, to carry water away without a stated direct object.
example: In the recorded intransitive drainage use, a channel that draws carries water away.
distinctions: Water is understood from the drainage context. The subject does not make an illustration.

originalSense.definition: Of a channel, drain, etc.: to carry water away.

definition: To flow or move rapidly along a path.
example: Water coursed through the narrow channel.
distinctions: The liquid or moving substance is the subject; this verb does not mean studying a course.

originalSense.definition: To run or flow (especially of liquids and more particularly blood).
originalSense.example: The oil coursed through the engine.

distinctionTask.prompt: Blood _____ through the vessels.
distinctionTask.explanation: Here courses means flows, with blood as its subject.

definition: To run through or over an area.
example: The hounds coursed the open fields.
distinctions: This transitive literary use describes covering an area; course after an animal instead describes pursuit.

originalSense.definition: To run through or over.

definition: To pursue prey by following or anticipating its route.
example: The hounds coursed the hare across the field.
distinctions: The pursued animal is the object. This differs from using course for liquid flowing through a channel.

originalSense.definition: To pursue by tracking or estimating the course taken by one's prey; to follow or chase after.
originalSense.example: We coursed him at the heels.

definition: To set an animal to chase game.
example: They coursed greyhounds after hares.
distinctions: The object is the pursuing animal, which someone sets to chase; the prey can follow after.

originalSense.definition: To cause to chase after or pursue game.

definition: (Informal speech) Of course.

originalSense.definition: Ellipsis of of course.

definition: The normal or customary development of events.
example: In the ordinary course of events, the report would be ready by Friday.
distinctions: The phrase describes what would normally happen, without prescribing a plan of action.

originalSense.definition: A normal or customary sequence.

definition: A chosen way of acting or proceeding.

distinctions: This course is an approach or decision, rather than a class, a physical path or a meal stage.

originalSense.definition: A programme, a chosen manner of proceeding.

distinctionTask.prompt: The committee chose a new _____ of action.
distinctionTask.explanation: A course of action is a chosen way to proceed.

definition: An ordered process or sequence of steps.
example: The investigation followed its prescribed course, from interviews to a final report.
distinctions: Here course organises successive stages; the treatment and education meanings name particular kinds of process.

originalSense.definition: Any ordered process or sequence of steps.

definition: A programme of organised learning.
example: The college offers a short course in first aid.

definition: A series of lessons or lectures on a subject.

originalSense.definition: a series of lectures or lessons in a particular subject

distinctionTask.prompt: She enrolled in a French _____ with ten weekly lessons.
distinctionTask.explanation: The organised series of lessons is a course.

definition: A college or university programme leading to a degree or vocational qualification.
example: His university course in engineering lasts four years.
distinctions: In this regional use, a course can cover an entire qualification. In American usage it more often means one subject class within a degree programme.
usage: Especially British, Irish and Philippine educational usage.

originalSense.definition: an educational programme at a college or university leading to an academic degree or vocational qualification.

definition: A planned sequence or period of medical treatment.
example: The doctor prescribed a short course of antibiotics.
distinctions: A course comprises the prescribed sequence or period; it is not the same as one dose.

originalSense.definition: A treatment plan.

distinctionTask.prompt: The prescription describes a _____ of treatment covering several days.
distinctionTask.explanation: A course covers the treatment sequence or period; a dose is one amount taken at a time.

definition: One stage of a meal, with its food served together.
example: Soup was served as the first course.
distinctions: A course is a stage of the meal. A dish is a particular prepared food and a meal may have several dishes in one course.

originalSense.definition: A stage of a meal.

distinctionTask.prompt: Soup arrived as the first _____ of the meal.
distinctionTask.explanation: A meal course is a stage of serving food.

definition: (Historical) A turn or succession in office or duty.
example: In the historical description of priests’ courses, each course takes its turn of duty.
distinctions: The source refers to an organised succession of duties; it does not describe an educational programme.

originalSense.definition: The succession of one to another in office or duty; order; turn.

definition: The route followed in a race.
example: The marathon course crosses the river twice.
distinctions: The course is the route competitors follow, rather than their finishing order.

originalSense.definition: The itinerary of a race.

distinctionTask.prompt: Runners followed the marked _____ through the park.
distinctionTask.explanation: The race course is the competitors’ route.

definition: A track or venue used for horse racing.
example: The horses were led onto the course before the race.
distinctions: This names the racing ground or track, while the itinerary sense can describe a route across a wider area.

originalSense.definition: A racecourse.

definition: The channel or route along which water flows.
example: The map shows the river’s old course.
distinctions: The watercourse is the channel or route, not the current or speed of the water.

originalSense.definition: The path taken by a flow of water; a watercourse.

definition: The trajectory followed by a ball or another thrown object.
example: The wind changed the course of the ball.
distinctions: This course is the object’s path through space; the whole playing area is a different sense.

originalSense.definition: The trajectory of a ball, frisbee etc.

definition: An area laid out with holes for playing golf.
example: The course has eighteen holes.
distinctions: The course is the playing area, not one stroke’s trajectory. Courses may have different numbers of holes, including nine or eighteen.

originalSense.definition: A golf course.

distinctionTask.prompt: Golfers walked from the ninth hole to the tenth on the _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A golf course is the playing area containing the holes.

definition: The direction in which a vessel is travelling.
example: The ship altered course to the east.
distinctions: Course describes direction of travel; heading describes where the vessel’s bow points. Wind and current can make them differ.

originalSense.definition: The direction of movement of a vessel at any given moment.

definition: The intended route of a ship, aircraft or other vehicle.
example: They plotted a course across the Atlantic.
collocations: set a course for a port
distinctions: A plotted course is an intended route; the actual track records where the vehicle travelled.

originalSense.definition: The intended passage of voyage, such as a boat, ship, airplane, spaceship, etc.

distinctionTask.prompt: Before departure, the navigator plotted a _____ across the ocean.
distinctionTask.explanation: A plotted course is the intended route.

definition: (Historical, India) A carriage drive at a station frequented by Europeans.
example: In the nineteenth-century Ferozepore passage, the course is a carriage drive at an Indian station used by Europeans.
collocations: on the course at a station
distinctions: The source describes a colonial social setting and uses station for the settlement or post, rather than a railway platform or an educational class.

originalSense.definition: The drive usually frequented by Europeans at an Indian station.

definition: A horizontal row of bricks or blocks in a wall.
example: The mason laid another course of bricks.
distinctions: A course runs along the wall. A vertical stack or column is not one horizontal course.

originalSense.definition: A row of bricks or blocks.

distinctionTask.prompt: The mason laid one horizontal _____ of bricks above another.
distinctionTask.explanation: A course is a horizontal row in the wall.

definition: A row of material in a roofing, waterproofing or flashing system.
example: The roofer overlapped each course of tiles with the one below.
distinctions: Course identifies a row of installed material; it does not itself specify a universal overlap size or installation method.

originalSense.definition: A row of material that forms the roofing, waterproofing or flashing system.

definition: A horizontal row of loops in weft-knitted fabric.
example: The knitter counted twenty courses in the sample.
distinctions: Courses run across the fabric; wales are the vertical columns of loops.

originalSense.definition: In weft knitting, a single row of loops connecting the loops of the preceding and following rows.

definition: The arrangement or sequence of people or things.
example: Put the names in alphabetical order.
distinctions: Order concerns arrangement; an order to do something is a command.

originalSense.definition: Arrangement, disposition, or sequence.
originalSense.example: put the children in age order

distinctionTask.prompt: Arrange these dates in chronological _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Chronological order means a sequence by time.

definition: A place within an arrangement or sequence.
example: In the historical geological description, each layer disappearing in its order refers to its particular place in the sequence.
distinctions: This sense concerns a place in the sequence. The whole arrangement is a related but broader use.
usage: Contextual reading of the preserved geological example.

originalSense.definition: A position in an arrangement, disposition, or sequence.
originalSense.example: In these situations we find the Genesee slate, the Tully limestone and the upper part of the Hamilton group, each one in its order disappearing beneath the lake level as we proceed southward.
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: A properly arranged or functioning state.
example: The engineer checked that the equipment was in working order.
distinctions: In order can describe an arranged state or proper functioning. Out of order on a machine means it is not working correctly.

originalSense.definition: The state of being well arranged.

wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

distinctionTask.prompt: The technician confirmed that the printer was in working _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: In working order means functioning properly.

definition: Public calm and observance of rules or lawful behaviour.
example: The stewards restored order after the disturbance.
distinctions: Order here concerns orderly conduct, rather than alphabetic arrangement or a purchase.

originalSense.definition: Conformity with law or decorum; freedom from disturbance; general tranquillity; public quiet.
originalSense.example: to preserve order in a community or an assembly
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

distinctionTask.prompt: The stewards restored _____ after the disturbance.
distinctionTask.explanation: Restoring order means restoring calm and orderly conduct.

definition: An authoritative command or instruction.
example: The captain gave the crew an order to return to port.
distinctions: The speaker directs an action. A purchase order instead requests goods or services.

originalSense.definition: A command.
originalSense.example: give an order
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

distinctionTask.prompt: The captain gave an _____ to return to port immediately.
distinctionTask.explanation: Here the order is an authoritative command.

definition: A request to buy, sell or supply goods or services.
example: We placed an order for two replacement parts.
distinctions: Place an order is the usual purchase collocation; a command given to another person uses a different sense.

originalSense.definition: A request for some product or service; a commission to purchase, sell, or supply goods.
originalSense.example: make an order
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

distinctionTask.prompt: We placed an _____ for two replacement parts.
distinctionTask.explanation: Place an order requests goods; an ordinance is a law or regulation.

definition: The goods supplied or prepared in response to a purchase request.
example: Your order has been packed and is ready for collection.
distinctions: This refers to the goods, rather than only the request used to buy them.

originalSense.definition: The goods requested.
originalSense.example: Your order should arrive within two days.
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

distinctionTask.prompt: Your _____ has been packed and is ready to collect.
distinctionTask.explanation: Here order refers to the purchased goods.

definition: A religious community whose members follow a shared rule or principles.
example: She joined a religious order that runs schools.
distinctions: This names an organised religious community; holy orders instead concerns ordained ministry.

originalSense.definition: A group of religious adherents, especially monks or nuns, set apart within their religion by adherence to a particular rule or set of principles.
originalSense.example: St. Ignatius Loyola founded the Jesuit order in 1537.
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: An association or body of knights.
example: The knight was admitted to the order.

originalSense.definition: An association of knights.
originalSense.example: the Order of the Garter, the Order of the Bath.
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: A body of people united by a shared interest or profession.
example: A reference to an order of physicians uses order for a body of people sharing a profession.
distinctions: This reading names an organised body of people, rather than a command, purchase request or numerical sequence.

originalSense.definition: Any group of people with common interests.
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: An honour or decoration awarded for distinguished service.
example: She was awarded the order for distinguished public service.
distinctions: An order can be a named honour with several grades; it is not necessarily a single generic medal or a command.

originalSense.definition: A decoration, awarded by a government, a dynastic house, or a religious body to an individual, usually for distinguished service to a nation or to humanity.

definition: A taxonomic rank below class and above family, or a taxon at that rank.
example: Magnolias are classified in the order Magnoliales.

originalSense.definition: A category in the classification of organisms, ranking below class and above family; a taxon at that rank.

definition: A rank, class, kind or level of people or things.

originalSense.definition: A number of things or persons arranged in a fixed or suitable place, or relative position; a rank; a row; a grade; especially, a rank or class in society; a distinct character, kind, or sort.

wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: An ecclesiastical rank or ordained ministry, especially in holy orders.
example: He was admitted to holy orders.

originalSense.definition: An ecclesiastical rank or position, usually for the sake of ministry, (especially, when plural) holy orders.
originalSense.example: There have been many major and minor orders in the history of Christianity: the order of virgins, of deacons, priests, lectors, acolytes, porters, catechists, widows, etc.
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: A classical architectural system governing columns and the structure they support.
example: The facade uses the Doric order.
distinctions: An architectural order includes proportions and details of columns and entablature; it is more than their left-to-right arrangement.

originalSense.definition: The disposition of a column and its component parts, and of the entablature resting upon it, in classical architecture; hence (since the column and entablature are the characteristic features of classical architecture) a style or manner of architectural design.
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: The sequence in which a cricket side’s batters bat.
example: The coach moved her up the batting order.

originalSense.definition: The sequence in which a side’s batsmen bat; the batting order.

definition: A scale, size or scope used in comparison.

originalSense.definition: Scale: size or scope.

wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: The degree of a relevant polynomial or transfer function used to characterise an electronic circuit or filter.

originalSense.definition: A power of polynomial function in an electronic circuit’s block, such as a filter, an amplifier, etc.

wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: For a power-law rate expression, the sum of the concentration exponents; individual exponents give orders with respect to each species.

definition: The number of elements of a set or algebraic structure.
example: The cyclic group has order four because it contains four elements.

distinctions: The order of a group counts all its elements. The order of one group element is the repetition count needed to reach the identity.

example: In the rotational symmetry group of a square, a quarter-turn has order four.
distinctions: Four quarter-turns give the identity rotation. An element has infinite order if no positive power gives the identity; its order is not the number of all elements in the group.

definition: The number of vertices in a graph.

originalSense.definition: The number of vertices in the graph (i.e. the set-theoretic order of the set of vertices of the graph).

distinctionTask.prompt: A graph has five vertices and seven edges. Its order is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Graph order counts vertices, while size commonly counts edges.

definition: A set equipped with a partial-order relation.

originalSense.definition: A partially ordered set.

definition: The relation used to partially order a set.
example: Set inclusion defines an order on these subsets.
distinctions: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. It need not compare every pair; that additional condition gives a total order.

originalSense.definition: The relation with which a partially ordered set is equipped.
wordFamily: Ancient and Honorable Order of Turtles

definition: The sum of a monomial’s variable exponents, also called its total degree.
example: The monomial x²y³z has order six.
distinctions: In x²y³z the exponents are 2, 3 and 1, so the total is 6. The coefficients are not included in that sum.

originalSense.definition: The sum of the exponents of the variables involved in the expression.

definition: The largest variable exponent in a nonzero polynomial in one variable, also called its degree.
example: The polynomial 4x³ + x has order three.
distinctions: For one variable, inspect the highest power with a nonzero coefficient. Do not add the exponents of separate terms.

originalSense.definition: The order of the leading monomial; (equivalently) the largest power of the variable involved in the given expression.

definition: A written payment direction or instrument authorising someone to receive money or property.

definition: To put things into a specified sequence.

definition: To arrange things in a proper or orderly state.

definition: To request goods or services, especially as a purchase.

definition: A condition or restriction attached to an agreement or arrangement.
