distinctionTask.prompt: Economy of words means _____.
options: concise expression with little unnecessary wording
the market value of a language
distinctionTask.answer: concise expression with little unnecessary wording
distinctionTask.explanation: This is frugal use of words, not national economic activity.

definition: In theology, the way God is understood to govern or order the world.
example: In theological writing, the economy of God concerns divine ordering of the world rather than a national market.
distinctions: This is a theological account or belief, not a measurable claim about national production. The imported Wikipedia-link debris is omitted from the teaching definition.

originalSense.definition: The method of divine government of the world. (See Economy (religion) on Wikipedia.Wikipedia )
originalSense.example: The economy of God is in Jesus Christ alone.

definition: The lower standard-fare class or section of passenger travel, especially on an aircraft or train.
example: Our seats are in economy rather than business class.
distinctions: Here economy names a travel class. It does not state the exact baggage allowance, comfort, emissions or fare for every carrier. The checked source labels this noun US.

originalSense.definition: The part of a commercial passenger airplane or train reserved for those paying the lower standard fares; economy class.

distinctionTask.prompt: Seats in economy refer to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Here economy is the name of a travel class.

definition: In archaic usage, management of one’s residence or household.
example: In this archaic residency sense, economy concerns managing a home rather than a country’s economic system.
distinctions: Residency here concerns the place where someone lives. It does not mean an immigration decision or a medical training post.

originalSense.definition: Management of one’s residency.

definition: Designed to use few resources, cost little to run or offer good value.
example: They chose an economy model to keep operating costs low.
distinctions: As an adjective, economy describes an economical or budget option in context. The label alone does not prove lower lifetime cost or better value for every user.

originalSense.definition: Cheap to run; using minimal resources; representing good value for money; economical.
originalSense.example: He bought an economy car.

distinctionTask.prompt: An economy model is presented as _____.
options: proof of the lowest lifetime cost for every buyer
distinctionTask.explanation: The description requires context and does not prove universal value.

definition: By economy class when travelling by air.
example: We plan to fly economy on the return journey.
distinctions: In fly economy, economy modifies the manner or class of travel. In in economy, it is a noun after a preposition. Both can describe the same class without the same grammatical construction.
usage: Adverbial use; checked source label US.

originalSense.definition: In or via the part of a commercial passenger airplane reserved for those paying the lower standard fares.
originalSense.example: Numerous web sites have tips on how to fly economy.

distinctionTask.prompt: In We fly economy, economy functions _____.
options: adverbially to describe the travel class
as the subject of the sentence
distinctionTask.answer: adverbially to describe the travel class
distinctionTask.explanation: We is the subject; economy describes how the travellers fly.

definition: In obsolete usage, the regular natural processes sustaining the life of animals or plants.
example: In older animal economy or vegetable economy, the term refers to life processes, not the financial activity of animals or plants.
distinctions: The source labels this biological arrangement sense obsolete. It should not be treated as the modern study of wildlife markets.

originalSense.definition: The regular operation of nature in the generation, nutrition and preservation of animals or plants.

definition: In obsolete usage, a system for regulating the affairs of a state, government or department.
example: In older government writing, economy can refer to the arrangement and regulation of public affairs.
distinctions: This historical administrative meaning is separate from the present economic system of production and consumption.

originalSense.definition: System of management; general regulation and disposition of the affairs of a state or nation, or of any department of government.

definition: In obsolete usage, a system of religious rules, rites or ceremonies.
example: In an older phrase such as the Jewish economy, economy can denote a system of religious observances.
distinctions: This historical sense concerns an ordered system of practices. It is not a statement about the finances of a religious or ethnic group.

originalSense.definition: A system of rules, regulations, rites and ceremonies.

definition: In obsolete usage, the arrangement or organisation of a work.
example: In older criticism, the economy of a poem can mean the arrangement of its parts.
distinctions: The source labels this arrangement meaning obsolete. Distinguish it from economy of words, which concerns avoiding unnecessary wording.

originalSense.definition: The disposition or arrangement of any work.

definition: The art or study of managing household resources, now chiefly called home economics.
example: In the older standalone household sense, economics concerns household management; home economics remains a current subject name.
distinctions: The checked source marks standalone economics in this sense dated. That does not make the modern phrase home economics obsolete. The academic social science and household finances are separate meanings.
usage: Dated standalone household-management sense; now chiefly home economics.

originalSense.definition: Now chiefly home economics: the art or science of household management, especially relating to the appropriate organization of resources; housekeeping.
originalSense.example: Thus Logick, Phyſicks, Metaphyſicks, are the burden of Volumes, and the dayly entertainment of the Diſputing Schools: vvhile the more profitable doctrines of the Heavens, Meteors, Minerals, Animals; as alſo the more practical ones of Politicks, and Oeconomicks, are ſcarce ſo much as glanc'd at.

definition: The study of how resources and wealth are allocated, produced, distributed and consumed.
example: Economics is the study of how people allocate scarce resources.
distinctions: Economics as an academic subject normally takes singular agreement: economics is. The economy is the actual system studied. The economics of an activity has a separate financial-aspects sense, usually with plural agreement.
usage: Social science; singular agreement for the field of study.

originalSense.definition: The study of resource and wealth allocation, consumption, and distribution, of capital and investment, and of management of the factors of production.
originalSense.example: Mary studied economics for five years before going into banking.

distinctionTask.prompt: Economics _____ a social science.
distinctionTask.explanation: The academic subject economics takes singular agreement.

definition: An obsolete plural of economic, referring to household managers or historical administrators of vacant church benefices.
example: The obsolete plural economics can refer to people called economics in older records, rather than to the modern academic discipline.
distinctions: This is a plural of a rare person noun. It is separate from both the singular subject economics and the financial-aspects construction the economics of.
usage: Obsolete plural of a person noun.

originalSense.definition: plural of economic (“one who is skilled in household management; (Christianity, historical) one who manages the income of a vacant benefice”).

definition: Management of household finances, or a household’s financial situation.
example: Higher rent has changed the household economics.
distinctions: This restored child concerns a household’s money management or position. It is narrower than home economics, which can also cover food, clothing and other household resources.

originalSense.definition: Management of household finances; also, the financial situation of a household.

distinctionTask.prompt: Household economics here concerns _____.
options: a household’s finances and their management
distinctionTask.answer: a household’s finances and their management
distinctionTask.explanation: The restored meaning is a household’s financial affairs, narrower than all household management.

definition: The application of economics to a particular field, usually named by a descriptive word.
example: Environmental economics examines choices about resources and pollution.
distinctions: A descriptive term identifies an application of the field of study. Environmental economics remains a singular subject; it is not identical to a particular country’s current financial situation.
usage: Applied field of study; normally singular agreement.

originalSense.definition: Chiefly with a descriptive word: the application of this study to a particular domain.

distinctionTask.prompt: Environmental economics is _____.
options: an application of economics to a particular domain
a synonym for a country’s current bank balance
distinctionTask.answer: an application of economics to a particular domain
distinctionTask.explanation: The descriptive word identifies an applied field of study.

definition: The financial situation of a nation, state or similar political unit.
example: In this source meaning, a nation’s economics refers to its financial situation rather than the academic study of economics.
distinctions: This source meaning describes a nation’s financial position. It is not the academic study of economics and does not reduce the whole economy to a single budget figure.

originalSense.definition: The financial situation of a nation, state, etc.

definition: The financial aspects or feasibility of an activity or enterprise, usually in the economics of something.
example: The economics of the project are uncertain because costs may rise.
distinctions: This financial-aspects sense usually takes plural agreement: the economics of the project are. Economics is for the academic subject uses singular agreement. Uncertain costs do not by themselves establish that a project must fail.
usage: Financial aspects; usually economics of; plural agreement.

originalSense.definition: Chiefly followed by of: the financial aspects of an activity, enterprise, etc.

distinctionTask.prompt: The economics of the project _____ uncertain because costs may rise.
distinctionTask.explanation: The financial-aspects meaning has plural agreement, unlike the singular field of study.

definition: To arise or follow as a consequence of a cause or process.
example: Delays can result from missing information.
distinctions: In A results from B, A is the effect and B is the cause or source. This reverses the grammatical order used by B results in A. The preposition determines which role follows the verb.

originalSense.definition: To proceed, spring up or rise, as a consequence, from facts, arguments, premises, combination of circumstances, consultation, thought or endeavor.
originalSense.example: Pleasure and peace do naturally result from a holy and good life.

distinctionTask.prompt: In Delays result from missing information, the roles are _____.
options: delays are the effect; missing information is the cause
delays are the cause; missing information is the effect
distinctionTask.answer: delays are the effect; missing information is the cause
distinctionTask.explanation: Result from introduces the cause after from.

definition: To lead to or produce a consequence, with in introducing the outcome.
example: Missing information can result in delays.
distinctions: In B results in A, B is the cause and A is the effect. Do not omit in before the outcome: result delays does not express this construction. Can leaves the particular outcome possible rather than guaranteed.

originalSense.definition: To have as a consequence; to lead to; to bring about
originalSense.example: This measure will result in good or in evil.

distinctionTask.prompt: In Missing information results in delays, the roles are _____.
options: missing information is the cause; delays are the effect
missing information is the effect; delays are the cause
distinctionTask.answer: missing information is the cause; delays are the effect
distinctionTask.explanation: Result in introduces the effect after in.

definition: In legal usage, to return to an owner or heirs following a reversion.
example: In this legal sense, property may result to a proprietor after a reversion; the word concerns a return of ownership.
distinctions: This is a specialised legal return sense, not result in an outcome. The checked revision explicitly marks it legal.

originalSense.definition: To return to the proprietor (or heirs) after a reversion.

definition: In obsolete usage, to spring or leap back; to rebound.
example: In older writing, a stone resulting with a bound is springing back rather than producing an outcome.
distinctions: The source labels this physical rebound verb obsolete. Modern result from and result in concern consequences rather than bouncing.

originalSense.definition: To leap back; to rebound.
originalSense.example: the huge round stone, resulting with a bound

definition: An outcome, effect, conclusion or value obtained from an action or process.
example: The result of adding 7 and 5 is 12.
distinctions: A result can be positive, negative or neutral. A test result is an observation or report, not automatically a diagnosis; an arithmetic result is obtained by the stated operation.

originalSense.definition: That which results; the conclusion or end to which any course or condition of things leads, or which is obtained by any process or operation; consequence or effect.
originalSense.example: the result of a course of action;  the result of a mathematical operation

7, because the result must be the first input

definition: A tangible or beneficial achievement produced by effort.

originalSense.definition: The final product, beneficial or tangible effect(s) achieved by effort.

a guarantee that any amount of effort succeeds

definition: A favourable outcome or success for someone.

the account holder has necessarily paid it

definition: To determine and demand the amount of tax due from a person or organisation.

proof that the tax has already been collected

definition: To examine something and reach a judgement about its quality, significance or value.

definition: In mathematics or computing, to work out the value of an expression.

definition: Of an expression or computation, to have or return a particular value.

definition: To perform mathematical computation or reckoning, without naming a direct object.

distinctionTask.prompt: In We calculate on paper, calculate _____.
options: has no direct object in this sentence
takes paper as its direct object
distinctionTask.answer: has no direct object in this sentence
distinctionTask.explanation: Paper belongs to the prepositional phrase on paper.

definition: In US dialect usage, to think, reckon, expect or plan.
example: In US dialect writing, I calculate can mean I reckon, I think or I expect, rather than I am doing arithmetic.
distinctions: The checked source labels this US dialect usage. It does not require numerical computation; retain the dialect context without claiming that all current uses of calculate mean expect.

It twisted and turned, and, the first thing I knew, made a sudden bend around a bunch of bayberry scrub and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn.

definition: To work out or forecast the timing, conditions or consequences of something by computation.
example: Astronomers calculate the timing of an eclipse from orbital data.

The broad source meaning also covers historical astrological calculations such as casting a nativity; that describes a belief practice, not an established method for predicting a person’s life. distinctionTask.prompt: An astronomer calculating an eclipse time uses _____.

a verified method for predicting a person’s life from a nativity

definition: To design, arrange or adapt something for a purpose or intended effect.

originalSense.definition: To adjust for purpose; to adapt by forethought or calculation; to fit or prepare by the adaptation of means to an end.

distinctionTask.prompt: Changes calculated to reduce waste are _____.
options: designed or arranged with that purpose
proof that waste has already fallen
distinctionTask.answer: designed or arranged with that purpose
distinctionTask.explanation: A stated purpose or expected effect does not establish an achieved result.

definition: In chess, to work through possible sequences of moves and replies mentally.
example: Before choosing a move, players calculate several possible replies.
distinctions: This chess sense concerns considering sequences without moving the pieces during the calculation. It is not merely counting pieces. An abstract branch diagram does not establish that a particular move is legal or best in an unspecified position.

originalSense.definition: To imagine sequences of potential moves and responses without actually moving the pieces.

distinctionTask.prompt: In chess, calculating a variation means _____.
options: considering possible moves and replies mentally
only counting how many pieces remain
distinctionTask.answer: considering possible moves and replies mentally
distinctionTask.explanation: The chess meaning is the mental analysis of possible continuations.

definition: To state or estimate that a future event will happen; also, to foretell an event as a prophecy.

usage: Transitive; a forecast or prophecy about a future event.

originalSense.definition: To make a prediction: to forecast, foretell, or estimate a future event on the basis of knowledge and reasoning; to prophesy a future event on the basis of mystical knowledge or power.

distinctionTask.prompt: A forecast predicting heavy rain tomorrow is _____.
options: a prediction whose outcome still needs observation
a guarantee that the rain will occur
distinctionTask.answer: a prediction whose outcome still needs observation
distinctionTask.explanation: A forecast concerns a future event and can be wrong.

definition: Of a theory, law or model, to imply a particular result under stated conditions.
example: For x = 3, the model y = 2x predicts y = 6.
distinctions: Here predict means that a result follows within a model or theory. With x = 3 and y = 2x, y = 6 follows mathematically; this alone does not establish a real-world observation. The implication need not concern a future event.
usage: Of theories, laws or models; implication under conditions.

originalSense.definition: To imply.
originalSense.example: It is interesting to see how clearly theory predicts the difference between the ascending and descending curves of a dynamo.

distinctionTask.prompt: For x = 3, the model y = 2x predicts y = 6. This states _____.
options: what follows within the stated model
proof that every real-world observation must equal 6
distinctionTask.answer: what follows within the stated model
distinctionTask.explanation: The model implication is conditional on its rule and input; observation is a separate matter.

definition: To make forecasts or predictions, without naming a direct object.
example: It is hard to predict accurately with so little information.
distinctions: In this sentence predict is intransitive: accurately is an adverb and no direct object names the predicted event. This does not mean predict can never take an object; predict heavy rain is transitive.

originalSense.definition: To make predictions.

definition: AIM as an initialism for AOL Instant Messenger.
example: In historical Internet writing, AIM names AOL Instant Messenger, the messaging service that operated from 1997 to 2017.
distinctions: This capitalised record names the historical service. It differs from the verb AIM meaning to send a message through that service and from other expansions of AIM.

originalSense.definition: Initialism of AOL Instant Messenger.

definition: AIM as an initialism for Aeronomy of Ice in the Mesosphere, a NASA satellite.
example: In this NASA satellite context, AIM expands to Aeronomy of Ice in the Mesosphere.
collocations: Aeronomy of Ice in the Mesosphere
distinctions: This expansion names a satellite and is distinct from Asteroid Impact Mission. The name alone does not establish the satellite’s present operating status.

originalSense.definition: Initialism of Aeronomy of Ice in the Mesosphere, a NASA satellite.

definition: AIM, the London Stock Exchange’s secondary stock market, formerly an initialism of Alternative Investment Market.
example: In UK finance, AIM names the London Stock Exchange’s secondary stock market; Alternative Investment Market is its former initialism expansion.
distinctions: The source qualifies the expansion with formerly. The name does not indicate the everyday noun aim, and listing alone does not establish an investment’s quality or return.

originalSense.definition: AIM, the secondary stock market of the London Stock Exchange; formerly an initialism of Alternative Investment Market.

definition: AIM as an initialism for American Indian Movement.
example: In this movement-name context, AIM expands to American Indian Movement.
distinctions: This is a particular movement’s name, distinct from Agape International Missions and the other AIM expansions. The ordinary noun aim can separately describe a movement’s goal.

originalSense.definition: Initialism of American Indian Movement.
originalSense.example: There are Schimmel Sister stickers, and Navajo Nation stickers, Cherokee Nation stickers, Idle No More, and AIM flags duct-taped to antennas.

definition: AIM as an acronym for air intercept missile.
example: In this US military context, AIM expands to air intercept missile.
distinctions: This expansion concerns a type of missile, rather than an organisation, space mission or the ordinary verb aim. It does not specify a particular model or its capabilities.

originalSense.definition: Acronym of air intercept missile.

definition: To communicate with someone through the former AIM messaging service.
example: In historical Internet writing, AIMed means sent a message or talked to someone through AOL Instant Messenger.
distinctions: This informal historical verb can take a person as its object or be used without a direct object. It is tied to the service of 1997–2017, rather than being a current general verb for every messaging app.

originalSense.definition: To talk to (someone) via the instant messaging service AIM (AOL Instant Messenger; 1997–2017); to send (someone) a message via this service.
originalSense.example: Um, alrighty then. Marcus likes me, we AIMed earlier and had really good cybersex. =Þ

definition: Facts or observations presented in support of an assertion.
example: The survey provides evidence of a change in travel habits.
distinctions: Evidence supports a claim but need not establish it conclusively. The strength and relevance of the survey still need assessment. Ordinary evidence is uncountable: some evidence or a piece of evidence, rather than an evidence.

originalSense.definition: Facts or observations presented in support of an assertion.
originalSense.example: There is no demonstrative evidence that anyone was here earlier.

distinctionTask.prompt: The survey is evidence for a claim. That means it _____.
options: provides support whose strength still needs assessment
automatically proves the claim beyond any doubt
distinctionTask.answer: provides support whose strength still needs assessment
distinctionTask.explanation: Evidence can be relevant support without being conclusive proof.

definition: Material admitted by a court to help prove or disprove alleged facts in a trial.
example: The court admitted the recording as evidence.
distinctions: Admission means the material may be considered under the applicable rules. It does not itself establish guilt, the truth of every statement in the recording, or the final outcome. Rules differ by jurisdiction.

originalSense.definition: Anything admitted by a court to prove or disprove alleged matters of fact in a trial.
originalSense.example: For Lothian and Borders Police, the early-morning raid had come at the end one of biggest investigations carried out by the force, which had originally presented a dossier of evidence on the murder of Jodi Jones to the Edinburgh procurator-fiscal, William Gallagher, on 25 November last year.

distinctionTask.prompt: A court admits a recording as evidence. This establishes _____.
options: that it may be considered under the applicable rules
that the accused has been found guilty
distinctionTask.answer: that it may be considered under the applicable rules
distinctionTask.explanation: Admissibility and the final finding are separate matters.

definition: A person who bears witness.
example: In the source quotation, evidences names people who bear witness, rather than the facts or observations they provide.
distinctions: This separate countable source meaning concerns a witness. Use witness in ordinary contemporary study sentences; do not transfer its plural to the uncountable support meaning. The source does not explicitly label this record obsolete.

originalSense.definition: One who bears witness.
originalSense.example: infamous and perjured evidences

definition: In a strict source formulation, a body of objectively verifiable facts indicating one conclusion rather than alternatives.
example: This source meaning uses evidence narrowly for a body of verifiable facts indicating one conclusion over alternatives.
distinctions: This is a stricter formulation than ordinary evidence. It must not make every instance of evidence conclusive, or imply that merely calling something evidence establishes the facts or excludes every alternative.

originalSense.definition: A body of objectively verifiable facts that are positively indicative of, and/or exclusively concordant with, that one conclusion over any other.

definition: To provide evidence for, or suggest the truth of, something.
example: The repeated requests evidence a need for clearer instructions.
distinctions: The verb means provide evidence for or indicate. The requests support an interpretation; they do not make that interpretation infallible. Evidence is a transitive verb here; as evidenced by uses a passive form.

originalSense.definition: To provide evidence for, or suggest the truth of.
originalSense.example: She was furious, as evidenced by her slamming the door.

distinctionTask.prompt: The requests evidence a need uses evidence as _____.
options: a verb meaning indicate or provide support for
a noun naming a person who gives testimony
distinctionTask.answer: a verb meaning indicate or provide support for
distinctionTask.explanation: The requests are the subject and a need is the object.

definition: A test or trial intended to establish or discover a fact.
example: The countable test meaning of proof names a trial or testing process, rather than the conclusive evidence it may produce.
distinctions: Carrying out a test does not establish that it passed. The source preserves this countable meaning separately from uncountable proof as conclusive evidence.

originalSense.definition: An effort, process, or operation designed to establish or discover a fact or truth; an act of testing; a test; a trial.
originalSense.example: I need proof of your unconditional love. Lend me some dough.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: Evidence or demonstration taken as establishing a fact or truth.
example: The missing signature is not proof that the document is a forgery.
distinctions: Proof is stronger than mere supporting evidence in this meaning, but what establishes a claim depends on the context and standard. A missing signature alone need not establish forgery. Ordinary conclusive proof is uncountable.

originalSense.definition: The degree of evidence which convinces the mind of any truth or fact, and produces belief; a test by facts or arguments which induce, or tend to induce, certainty of the judgment; conclusive evidence; demonstration.
originalSense.example: I'll have some proof.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: The missing signature is not proof of forgery. This says _____.
options: that fact alone does not establish forgery
the document has been conclusively shown genuine
distinctionTask.answer: that fact alone does not establish forgery
distinctionTask.explanation: Lack of proof for one claim does not prove its opposite.

definition: The quality of having been tested and resisting force or impression.
example: In this physical-quality meaning, proof concerns tested firmness or resistance, rather than a logical demonstration.
distinctions: The source preserves a physical quality. Do not infer complete resistance to every force or use it as a modern engineering rating without specified test conditions.

originalSense.definition: The quality or state of having been proved or tried; firmness or hardness which resists impression, or does not yield to force; impenetrability of physical bodies.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: An obsolete meaning: experience of something.
example: In the older quotation, proof refers to experience, not a printing sheet or an argument establishing a theorem.
distinctions: The source marks the experience meaning obsolete. Modern proof of experience would usually mean evidence that someone has experience, a different construction.

originalSense.definition: Experience of something.
originalSense.example: But the chaste damzell, that had never priefe / Of such malengine and fine forgerye, / Did easely beleeve her strong extremitye.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: An obsolete meaning: firmness of mind or unshakable resolve.
example: This older proof describes firmness of mind, rather than evidence supporting a belief.
distinctions: The source marks this mental-firmness meaning obsolete. Firm conviction is not itself proof that a belief is true.

originalSense.definition: Firmness of mind; stability not to be shaken.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: A trial printed impression or sheet used for checking and correction.
example: The editor marked a spelling error on the proof before publication.
distinctions: A printing proof is a version for checking. It can contain errors and is separate from conclusive evidence or the final published copy.

originalSense.definition: A proof sheet; a trial impression, as from type, taken for correction or examination.
originalSense.example: And these men scour the printed proof for error, blunder, and misspelling.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: The editor corrects a printing proof. The proof is _____.
options: a trial version that may contain errors
distinctionTask.answer: a trial version that may contain errors
distinctionTask.explanation: A printing proof is made for examination and correction.

definition: A specially made, high-quality coin strike, now commonly produced for collectors.
example: The collector examined a proof from the new coin set.
distinctions: Proof describes the special method or quality of the strike. It does not inherently mean the coin has circulated, is unique, or will increase in financial value.

originalSense.definition: A limited-run high-quality strike of a particular coin, originally as a test run, although nowadays mostly for collectors' sets.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: A proof in a collectors’ coin set is _____.
options: necessarily a coin worn by circulation
distinctionTask.explanation: Proof concerns the special strike; circulation and value require separate information.

definition: A logical sequence from stated premises to the proposition being established.
example: For any integer n, 2n is divisible by 2; this is a proof that 2n is even.
distinctions: The definition of even is divisibility by 2. The premise that n is an integer supplies the needed domain. One example such as n = 3 alone would not prove the claim for every integer.

originalSense.definition: A sequence of statements consisting of axioms, assumptions, statements already demonstrated in another proof, and statements that logically follow from previous statements in the sequence, and which concludes with a statement that is the object of the proof.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: For every integer n, 2n is divisible by 2. The proof that 2n is even uses _____.
options: the definition of even and the stated integer domain
only a numerical check at n = 3
distinctionTask.answer: the definition of even and the stated integer domain
distinctionTask.explanation: A general proof applies to every integer in the stated domain.

definition: A check on the accuracy of a performed arithmetic operation.
example: After 48 ÷ 6 = 8, multiplying 8 by 6 gives 48 as a proof of the division.
distinctions: This checks the stated division by reversing it with multiplication. It does not by itself prove the correctness of every division algorithm or every calculation.

originalSense.definition: A process for testing the accuracy of an operation performed. Compare prove, transitive verb, 5.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: Checking 48 ÷ 6 = 8 by 8 × 6 = 48 checks _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: An inverse-operation check has a limited stated scope.

definition: An obsolete meaning: armour of tested quality, considered resistant to penetration.
example: In older writing, lapped in proof describes someone clothed in armour of tried quality.
distinctions: The source marks this armour noun obsolete. The historical judgement does not establish resistance to every weapon or modern ballistic certification.

originalSense.definition: Armour of excellent or tried quality, and deemed impenetrable; properly, armour of proof.
originalSense.example: Till that Bellona's bridegroom, lapped in proof
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: An alcohol-strength scale: in the United States, twice the alcohol percentage by volume.
example: On the US scale, 80 proof corresponds to 40% alcohol by volume.
distinctions: US proof is twice ABV. The historical British scale was different: 100 proof was about 57.1% ABV. Do not read 80 proof as 80% ABV or combine the two scales.
usage: US scale; historical British scale retained for comparison.

originalSense.definition: A measure of the alcohol content of liquor. Originally, in Britain, 100 proof was defined as 57.1% by volume (no longer used). In the US, 100 proof means that the alcohol content is 50% of the total volume of the liquid; thus, perfectly pure absolute alcohol would be 200 proof.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: A spirit labelled 80 proof on the US scale has _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: US proof is twice the alcohol percentage by volume.

definition: Used for testing or proving something.
example: The laboratory applied a proof load during the structural test.
distinctions: Proof modifies load: the load is used in a test. The phrase alone supplies no load value, safety factor, test result or rating for later use.

originalSense.definition: Used in proving or testing.
originalSense.example: a proof load; a proof charge
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: In proof load, proof describes _____.
options: the conclusive result of a test that always passed
distinctionTask.explanation: The adjective describes use; no result follows from the label.

definition: Resistant to the specified harm or influence.
example: She seemed proof against flattery.
distinctions: Proof against names resistance to the specified influence. Here seemed makes it an impression, and it does not mean she is resistant to every influence or that a belief is logically proved.

originalSense.definition: Firm or successful in resisting.
originalSense.example: proof against harm
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: She seemed proof against flattery means _____.
options: every claim she made was mathematically proved
distinctionTask.explanation: This adjective concerns resistance to a specified influence.

definition: Having a stated alcohol strength on a proof scale.
example: The US label describes the spirit as 80-proof.
distinctions: The adjectival number uses a proof scale, not a percentage sign. On the US scale 80-proof means 40% ABV. The historical British scale uses a different conversion.

originalSense.definition: Being of a certain standard as to alcohol content.
originalSense.example: 60% proof liquor
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: An 80-proof spirit on a US label uses _____.
options: a statement that 80% of the liquid is alcohol
distinctionTask.explanation: A proof number is not the same as the ABV percentage.

definition: To read and check text for errors; to proofread.
example: Please proof the final page before it is printed.
distinctions: Proof means check the text here. It does not certify that every factual claim is true or refer to making a material resistant to water.

originalSense.definition: To proofread.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: Please proof the page asks someone to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The text context selects the proofreading verb.

definition: To make something resistant, especially to water.
example: The treatment is intended to proof the fabric against water.
distinctions: Proof is a treatment verb here, not proofreading. Intended to does not establish that the treatment worked, and actual resistance depends on the material and conditions.

originalSense.definition: To make resistant, especially to water.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: A treatment intended to proof fabric against water aims to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The material and water context select the resistance-treatment verb.

definition: To subject a firearm to a specialised high-pressure test to establish its resistance to service pressures.
example: In firearms terminology, proof names a specialised pressure test rather than a routine accuracy test.
distinctions: This source meaning concerns testing resistance to pressure. It does not establish aim accuracy, the absence of every defect, or unlimited resistance under all conditions.

originalSense.definition: To test-fire with a load considerably more powerful than the firearm in question's rated maximum chamber pressure, in order to establish the firearm's ability to withstand pressures well in excess of those expected in service without bursting.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: To allow yeast-containing dough to rise, especially after shaping.
example: The baker will proof the shaped rolls before baking.
distinctions: This baking verb concerns dough rising. It differs from testing yeast activity, even though active yeast contributes to the rise; timing depends on the recipe and conditions.

originalSense.definition: To allow (yeast-containing dough) to rise, especially after it has been shaped
originalSense.example: dough proofing
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: Proof the shaped rolls asks for _____.
options: a separate test of yeast before any dough exists
distinctionTask.explanation: Dough rising and a yeast-activity test are separate baking uses.

definition: To test whether yeast is active.
example: The baker will proof the yeast before mixing the dough.
distinctions: Testing yeast activity and allowing shaped dough to rise are separate operations. The sentence gives no universal requirement to test every yeast product or a particular method or temperature.

originalSense.definition: To test the activeness of (yeast).
originalSense.example: yeast proofing
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: Proof the yeast before mixing the dough means _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The object yeast selects the activity-test meaning.

definition: Proof: the English title of the 98th sura, or chapter, of the Qur’an.
example: Capitalised Proof names the 98th chapter of the Qur’an in this source entry.
distinctions: This proper name retains the capitalised source identity. It is separate from lowercase proof meaning conclusive evidence and is not an assertion about the truth of a particular argument.

originalSense.definition: The 98th sura (chapter) of the Qur'an.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: A process of reasoning or argumentation.
example: Through careful argument, she challenged the proposed rule.
distinctions: This meaning concerns reasoning as a process. A challenge need not be angry, and the existence of a line of argument does not establish that it is sound or persuasive.

originalSense.definition: A process of reasoning; argumentation.
originalSense.example: Indeed, I cannot commend my life; for I am conſcious to my ſelf of many failings: therein, I know alſo that a man by his converſation, may ſoon overthrow what by argument or perſwaſion he doth labour to faſten upon others for their good: […]

distinctionTask.prompt: Careful argument used to challenge a rule refers to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Reasoning and quarrelling are separate meanings.

definition: A prefatory summary of a literary work or section; figuratively, its contents.
example: A literary argument can be a summary printed before a poem or chapter; the source also records a figurative extension to the contents themselves.
distinctions: The literary summary is separate from a disagreement or a logical reason. The figurative extension is retained within this source record rather than silently removed.

originalSense.definition: An abstract or summary of the content of a literary work such as a book, a poem or a major section such as a chapter, included in the work before the content itself; (figuratively) the contents themselves.
originalSense.example: If I would broach the veſſels of my loue, / And try the argument of hearts, by borrowing, / Men, and mens fortunes, could I frankely vſe / As I can bid thee ſpeake.

definition: A verbal disagreement or quarrel.
example: They had an argument about where to park.
distinctions: This sense concerns disagreement between people. It is different from an argument for a policy, which may simply be a reason; a verbal argument need not become physical.

originalSense.definition: A verbal dispute; a quarrel.
originalSense.example: The neighbours got into an argument about the branches of the trees that extended over the fence.

distinctionTask.prompt: They had an argument about parking means they _____.
options: supplied a value to a mathematical function
distinctionTask.explanation: The people and disagreement context select the quarrel meaning.

definition: By humorous or euphemistic extension, a dispute, altercation or collision.
example: The report jokingly called the van’s collision with a bollard an argument.
distinctions: The source allows a jocular or euphemistic extension beyond words. The bollard does not literally speak, and the wording should not conceal whether an actual collision occurred.

originalSense.definition: Any dispute, altercation, or collision.
originalSense.example: Steve got in a physical argument with his neighbor and came away with a black eye.

distinctionTask.prompt: Calling a van’s collision with a bollard an argument is _____.
options: a jocular extension beyond a verbal disagreement
a literal conversation between the van and bollard
distinctionTask.answer: a jocular extension beyond a verbal disagreement
distinctionTask.explanation: The source preserves humorous and euphemistic extensions.

definition: In linguistics, a phrase syntactically connected to a clause’s verb as an argument.
example: In “Maya opened the door”, the phrase “the door” is an argument of “opened”.
distinctions: In this English example, the door is an object argument, while an added yesterday is a time adjunct. Arguments are not defined simply as every nearby word or every phrase that cannot be omitted. Analyses and constructions vary.

originalSense.definition: Any of the phrases that bear a syntactic connection to the verb of a clause.
originalSense.example: In numerous works over the past two decades, beginning with the pioneering work of Gruber (1965), Fillmore (1968a), and Jackendoff (1972), it has been argued that each Argument (i.e. Subject or Complement) of a Predicate bears a particular thematic role (alias theta-role, or θ-role to its Predicate), and that the set of thematic functions which Arguments can fulfil are drawn from a highly restricted, finite, universal set.

distinctionTask.prompt: In Maya opened the door yesterday, the door is an object argument, while yesterday is _____.
options: a time adjunct in this example
another object argument merely because it is nearby
distinctionTask.answer: a time adjunct in this example
distinctionTask.explanation: Syntactic role, rather than proximity, distinguishes this example.

definition: The independent variable of a function.
example: In f(x) = x², x is the argument of f.
distinctions: The argument supplies the function’s input. It differs from the output f(x); at x = 3 the input is 3 and the output is 9. This mathematical use need not involve a software function call.

originalSense.definition: The independent variable of a function.

distinctionTask.prompt: In f(x) = x² at x = 3, the argument value and output are _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The argument is the input; f(3) is the output.

definition: The phase angle of a complex number.
example: The complex number 1 + i has principal argument π/4 radians.
distinctions: The modulus of 1 + i is √2, not π/4. Its arguments differ by integer multiples of 2π; a principal argument selects a branch convention. Zero has no defined argument.

originalSense.definition: The phase of a complex number.

distinctionTask.prompt: For 1 + i, principal argument π/4 names _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Complex argument is phase angle, not magnitude.

definition: A quantity on which the calculation of another quantity depends.
example: In the refraction table, altitude is the argument used to look up the correction.
distinctions: The argument is the input used in the table or calculation, not the resulting correction. A table’s stated conditions matter; the wording alone gives no universal refraction formula.

originalSense.definition: A quantity on which the calculation of another quantity depends.
originalSense.example: The altitude is the argument of the refraction.

distinctionTask.prompt: Altitude used as an argument in a correction table is _____.
options: the input used to look up the correction
necessarily the correction returned by the table
distinctionTask.answer: the input used to look up the correction
distinctionTask.explanation: The argument is an input quantity.

definition: A value, or reference to a value, supplied to a function.
example: In the call square(3), 3 is the argument.
distinctions: In a definition such as square(x), x is a formal parameter; 3 is the argument supplied in the call. Languages differ in how values or references are passed.

originalSense.definition: A value, or a reference to a value, passed to a function.
originalSense.example: Parameters are like labelled fillable blanks used to define a function whereas arguments are passed to a function when calling it, filling in those blanks.

distinctionTask.prompt: Given definition square(x) and call square(3), the argument is _____.
options: 3, while x is a formal parameter
x, while 3 is the definition’s formal name
distinctionTask.answer: 3, while x is a formal parameter
distinctionTask.explanation: The roles are supplied argument and named formal parameter.

definition: An actual parameter supplied in a function call, rather than a formal parameter in its definition.
example: In add(2, 5), each supplied number is an argument, also called an actual parameter.
distinctions: If the definition is add(a, b), a and b are the formal parameters. The call supplies arguments 2 and 5. The older term actual parameter does not make the formal name and supplied value the same role.
usage: Programming; terminology overlaps with the value sense.

originalSense.definition: A parameter at a function call; an actual parameter, as opposed to a formal parameter.

distinctionTask.prompt: In add(2, 5), actual parameters are _____.
options: only the formal names in add(a, b)
distinctionTask.explanation: Actual parameter is an alternative term for a supplied argument.

definition: An obsolete meaning: the matter in question or business at hand.
example: In older writing, argument can name the matter being considered, rather than a quarrel or function input.
distinctions: This child meaning inherits the source’s obsolete heading. A modern reason supporting a proposition remains a separate use.

originalSense.definition: A matter in question; a business in hand.
originalSense.example:
As neere as I could ſift him on that argument,
 On ſome apparent danger ſeene in him,
 Aimde at your highnes, no inueterate malice.

definition: An obsolete meaning: the subject matter or theme of a work, discourse or representation.
example: In the older thematic use, argument names what a work or discourse is about.
distinctions: This thematic child inherits the source’s obsolete heading. It differs from the independently preserved literary prefatory summary.

originalSense.definition: The subject matter of an artistic representation, discourse, or writing; a theme or topic.
originalSense.example: [I]n vttering the ſtuffe ye receiued of the one, in declaring the order ye tooke with the other, ye ſhall neuer lacke, neither matter, nor maner, what to write, nor how to write in this kinde of Argument.

definition: An archaic meaning: evidence or proof, including a countable item of it.
example: In this older use, argument can mean evidence or proof; a particular item can be an argument.
distinctions: The source marks the broad use archaic and retains a countable item extension. Do not apply the countable grammar to ordinary uncountable evidence or treat every modern argument as conclusive proof.
usage: Archaic noun; countable item extension retained.

originalSense.definition: Evidence, proof; (countable) an item of such evidence or proof.
originalSense.example: [F]or louing me, by my troth it is no addition to her wit, nor no great argument of her follie, for I will be horribly in loue with her, […]

definition: To put forward an argument; to argue.
example: The source’s older verb argument describes arguing, rather than passing a software function an input.
distinctions: The source labels this intransitive verb obsolete and now nonstandard in some learner usage. Use argue in standard modern writing. Its label does not make the ordinary noun obsolete.
usage: Obsolete; now nonstandard in the source’s stated usage.

originalSense.definition: To put forward as an argument; to argue.
originalSense.example: [I]t is moſt certaine, that after Herodotus and other auncient writers, it is ſafer to call theſe [elephants' tusks] teeth, then hornes; and I will breefly ſet downe the reaſons of Philoſtratus, that will haue them to be teeth, and afterward of Grapaldus [i.e., Francesco Mario Grapaldi], Aelianus, and Pauſanias, that would make them horns, and ſo leaue the reader to conſider whether opinion he thinketh moſt agreeable to truth. […] Thus they argument for the horns of Elephants.

definition: An obsolete verb meaning: to adduce evidence or provide proof.
example: In the older source use, argument as a verb concerns providing evidence or proof.
distinctions: The source labels this intransitive verb obsolete. Keep it separate from both ordinary argue and the modern noun naming a reason or a function input.

originalSense.definition: To adduce evidence, to provide proof.
originalSense.example: Albeit that it apperteneth to the apoſtolis, be the puiſtoun of God to tak ordour in all materis off debait cõcernyng ye faith, & ſpecialie to iterprete ye ſcripturis, as yat quhilkis had yͤ ſpreit of god, & wer yͤ trew kirk: It argumẽtis [argumentis] not yat vtheris, quha hes ꝯuenit [conuenit] ſenſyne in generale ꝯſales [consales] had the ſpreit of GOD, or wer the trew kirk: […]

definition: In logic, premises arranged with a conclusion intended to follow from them.
example: All squares are rectangles; this figure is a square; therefore it is a rectangle: this is a valid argument.
distinctions: An argument can be invalid, or have false premises. Validity concerns whether the conclusion follows; soundness also requires true premises. The stated example uses the standard inclusive definition of rectangle.
usage: Logic and philosophy; restored child meaning.

originalSense.definition: A series of propositions organized so that the final proposition is a conclusion which is intended to follow logically from the preceding propositions, which function as premises.

distinctionTask.prompt: An argument is valid when _____.
options: its conclusion follows logically from its premises
every premise is guaranteed true merely by being written
distinctionTask.answer: its conclusion follows logically from its premises
distinctionTask.explanation: Validity concerns the logical relation; soundness additionally requires true premises.

definition: A belief, judgement or perspective formed about a topic, person or thing.
example: In my opinion, the revised plan is more practical.
distinctions: An opinion can be informed by evidence or reflect subjective judgement. Calling it an opinion does not by itself make it false, baseless or beyond criticism. An opinion is not automatically conclusive proof.
usage: Countable or uncountable according to construction.

originalSense.definition: A belief, judgment or perspective that a person has formed, either through objective or subjective reasoning, about a topic, issue, person or thing.
originalSense.example: I would like to know your opinions on the new filing system.

distinctionTask.prompt: An informed opinion can _____.
options: draw on evidence while remaining a judgement
distinctionTask.answer: draw on evidence while remaining a judgement
