definition: A particular aspect, detail or respect.
example: The two plans are alike in cost but differ in this regard: travel time.
distinctions: This regard identifies an aspect of comparison. It does not refer to a steady look or to the esteem in which a person is held.
usage: Noun; usually preceded by in or with.

originalSense.definition: A particular aspect or detail; respect, sense.
originalSense.example: This attempt will be made with every regard to the difficulty of the undertaking […]

distinctionTask.prompt: The plans differ in this regard: travel time. Regard identifies _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Travel time names the relevant respect or detail.

definition: The esteem or estimation in which someone or something is held.
example: Her colleagues hold her in high regard.
distinctions: High regard concerns esteem. It does not mean colleagues are physically looking at the person or that every judgement about her is correct.
usage: Uncountable noun; hold someone in high regard.

originalSense.definition: The worth or estimation in which something or someone is held.
originalSense.example:
Dolph. For the Dolphin,
I stand here for him: what to him from England?
Exe. Scorne and defiance, sleight regard, contempt,
And any thing that may not mis-become
The mightie Sender, doth he prize you at.

distinctionTask.prompt: Her colleagues hold her in high regard. They _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The construction expresses estimation rather than visual observation.

definition: To look at or observe someone or something.
example: He regarded the damaged frame carefully.
distinctions: Here regard directs a look at an object. Regard something as useful instead expresses a judgement about it.
usage: Transitive; regard an object or person.

originalSense.definition: To look at; to observe.
originalSense.example: She regarded us warily.

distinctionTask.prompt: He regarded the damaged frame carefully. In this context he _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A careful look alone does not certify a condition.

definition: To consider or look upon someone or something in a stated way.
example: The council regards the park as a public asset.
distinctions: Regard as expresses a judgement or interpretation. It does not mean simply looking at the park, and the judgement is not independent proof.

originalSense.definition: To consider, look upon (something) in a given way etc.
originalSense.example: I always regarded tabloid journalism as a social evil.

distinctionTask.prompt: The council regards the park as a public asset. This states _____.
options: how the council considers the park
where the council is physically looking
distinctionTask.answer: how the council considers the park
distinctionTask.explanation: Regard as introduces the stated assessment.

definition: An archaic use meaning to take notice of or pay attention to.
example: In an older passage, regard him not can mean do not pay attention to him. It is separate from the modern regard him as construction.
collocations: regard him not in older prose
distinctions: This attention meaning is archaic. Modern regard him as introduces a judgement instead.

originalSense.definition: To take notice of, pay attention to.
originalSense.example: If much you note him / You ſhall offend him, and extend his Paſſion, / Feed, and regard him not.
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

definition: To face towards something.
example: In descriptions of buildings or places, regard can identify the direction they face, such as towards a river. It need not describe a person looking deliberately.
distinctions: Directional regard identifies orientation. Facing a direction does not establish an unobstructed view.
usage: Directional meaning; reading guidance for descriptions of places.

originalSense.definition: To face toward.
originalSense.example: Seated on a peninſula which regardeth the maine land ; ſtrong by nature, and fortified by Art : adorned heretofore with magnificent buildings ; and numbered amongſt the paradiſes of the earth, for temperate aire, and delightfull ſituation.

definition: To have to do with or concern something.
example: As it regards the administration of justice means as it concerns that topic. It differs from regarding something as valuable.
distinctions: This construction concerns relevance. Concerns or relates to often makes the intended meaning clearer in current prose.

originalSense.definition: To have to do with, to concern.
originalSense.example: That argument does not regard the question.

definition: An obsolete use meaning to value, esteem or respect someone or something.
example: In an older passage, regarding gain can mean valuing it or setting store by it. This is not simply looking at a gain.
distinctions: This value or respect verb meaning is obsolete. The ordinary modern noun high regard remains separate.
usage: Obsolete and transitive; historical reading guidance.

originalSense.definition: To set store by (something), to hold (someone) in esteem; to consider to have value, to respect.
originalSense.example: Ther was a Iudge in a certayne cite which feared not god nether regarded man.

definition: An Internet filter-avoidance spelling of the derogatory noun retard.
example: Some online writers deliberately use regard to evade a filter while invoking the derogatory insult. Context distinguishes this usage from the ordinary words for esteem or consideration.
distinctions: This deliberate online substitution retains the derogatory force of the insult. It is unsuitable as a neutral label for a person.
usage: Internet slang; reading guidance for recognising deliberate filter avoidance.

originalSense.definition: Filter-avoidance spelling of retard.

definition: Visual perception: seeing something or having it within sight.
example: The screen blocked our view of the doorway.
distinctions: This physical meaning concerns sight. More specific uses distinguish seeing, visible range, scenery and counted online viewings.
usage: Physical noun; view of something, a clear view or come into view.

originalSense.definition: Visual perception.
originalSense.example: He changed seats to get a complete view of the stage.

distinctionTask.prompt: A screen blocks our view of the doorway. It obstructs _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This physical context selects sight rather than a judgement.

definition: A drawn or painted picture or sketch of something.
example: The artist painted a view of the old harbour.
distinctions: Here a view is a representation created by an artist. The scenery itself is a separate view meaning.
usage: Noun; a view can mean a picture.

originalSense.definition: A picture, drawn or painted; a sketch.
originalSense.example: a fine view of Lake George

distinctionTask.prompt: The artist painted a view of the harbour. The view here is _____.
options: the harbour’s physical range of vision
distinctionTask.explanation: The context explicitly identifies a picture.

definition: An opinion, judgement, mental conception, idea or belief.
example: Her view was that the timetable needed changing.
distinctions: This mental meaning concerns thought rather than physical sight. More specific uses distinguish a mental image, an opinion, a perspective and an intention.
usage: Noun; hold a view about something or form a view.

originalSense.definition: An opinion, judgement, imagination, idea or belief.
originalSense.example: I need more information to get a better view of the situation.

distinctionTask.prompt: Her view was that the timetable needed changing. View expresses _____.
options: a picture drawn on the timetable
distinctionTask.explanation: The clause supplies the content of her judgement.

definition: In a relational database, a virtual or logical table defined by a query’s result.
example: The analyst created a view that shows only active accounts.
distinctions: An ordinary database view represents the result of its defining query. This does not assert an independent stored copy; a materialized view is a distinct implementation concept.

originalSense.definition: A virtual or logical table composed of the result set of a query in relational databases.

distinctionTask.prompt: An ordinary database view shows the result of a query over account records. It is _____.
options: a logical table defined by that query
necessarily a separately stored copy of every account
distinctionTask.answer: a logical table defined by that query
distinctionTask.explanation: The source defines a virtual or logical query result; materialization is a separate concept.

definition: The visible, interactive part of a computer program presented to its user.
example: The search view contains a text box and a results list.
distinctions: This view concerns the program’s interface. It need not be a database view or the underlying stored data.

originalSense.definition: The part of a computer program which is visible to the user and can be interacted with.

distinctionTask.prompt: A search view contains a text box and a results list. View here refers to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The controls and results identify a program interface.

definition: A wake.
example: The linked dictionary also gives view the noun meaning a wake, without an example. The surrounding passage is needed to identify the intended wake.
distinctions: This brief gloss needs context. It should not be replaced automatically with the usual sight or opinion meanings.
usage: Reading guidance; the linked definition does not supply an example.

originalSense.definition: A wake.

definition: To look at or watch something.
example: We viewed the flat on Saturday before deciding whether to rent it.
distinctions: Viewing the flat means looking at it. It does not establish that a rental decision or agreement followed.
usage: Transitive; view an object, place or recording.

originalSense.definition: To look at.
originalSense.example: The video was viewed by millions of people.

distinctionTask.prompt: We viewed the flat before deciding whether to rent it. The sentence establishes _____.
options: that we looked at the flat
that we signed a rental agreement
distinctionTask.answer: that we looked at the flat
distinctionTask.explanation: Looking at a property is separate from agreeing to rent it.

definition: To regard or interpret someone or something in a stated way.
example: They view the delay as a chance to revise the plan.
distinctions: View as introduces an interpretation. It need not describe physical seeing, and another person can interpret the same delay differently.

originalSense.definition: To regard in a stated way.
originalSense.example: I view it as a serious breach of trust.

distinctionTask.prompt: They view the delay as a chance to revise the plan. This tells us _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: View as supplies an assessment rather than a visual property.

definition: The act of seeing or looking at something.
example: Move a little so I can get a clear view of the demonstration.
distinctions: Here view concerns seeing the demonstration. It is not a drawn picture of it or an opinion about its quality.
usage: Physical noun; seeing or looking at something.

originalSense.definition: The act of seeing or looking at something.

distinctionTask.prompt: I move to get a clear view of the demonstration. I want _____.
options: to state a theory about it
distinctionTask.explanation: The physical movement supports seeing rather than an opinion.

definition: The range or field within which something can be seen.
example: The cyclist disappeared from view behind the wall.
distinctions: From view identifies the observer’s range of sight. Disappearing from sight does not establish that the cyclist stopped existing or reached a destination.
usage: Physical noun; the range of vision.

originalSense.definition: The range of vision.

distinctionTask.prompt: The cyclist disappeared from view behind a wall. The cyclist is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The obstruction concerns sight, not the cyclist’s motion.

definition: Something that can be looked at, especially scenery.
example: The room has a view of the river.
distinctions: This view is the visible scene. A painted view of the same river is a separate representation meaning.
usage: Physical noun; scenery or another scene to look at.

originalSense.definition: Something to look at, such as scenery.

distinctionTask.prompt: The room has a view of the river through its window. View refers to _____.
options: a required painting on the wall
distinctionTask.explanation: The window context identifies scenery.

definition: An individual user viewing of a web page, video or similar online content.
example: The report counted three video views from two viewers, including one repeat.
distinctions: Views count viewing events under the report’s counting rules. A repeat can make the view count larger than the number of distinct viewers; the definition does not set every platform’s threshold.
usage: Internet noun; a counted viewing event.

originalSense.definition: An individual viewing of a web page or a video etc. by a user.

distinctionTask.prompt: A report counts three views, one of them a repeat by the same viewer. Three views establish _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The repeat prevents equating event count with unique viewer count.

definition: An obsolete noun meaning appearance, show or aspect.
example: In older prose, view can describe an appearance, show or aspect. This particular meaning is obsolete.
distinctions: The appearance meaning is obsolete. The ordinary scenery and opinion meanings remain current.

originalSense.definition: Appearance; show; aspect.

definition: A mental image or conception of something.
example: The briefing gave us a clearer view of how the parts fit together.
collocations: form a view of the situation
distinctions: This view concerns a mental conception. A clearer conception need not be a literal picture or guarantee complete accuracy.
usage: Mental noun; a mental image or conception.

originalSense.definition: A mental image.

distinctionTask.prompt: A briefing gives us a clearer view of how the parts fit together. It improves _____.
options: our mental conception of the arrangement
distinctionTask.answer: our mental conception of the arrangement
distinctionTask.explanation: The context concerns understanding the arrangement.

definition: A way of understanding something, an opinion or a theory.
example: My view is that the library should stay open later.
distinctions: This is an opinion about desired opening hours. It does not report the library’s current closing time.
usage: Mental noun; an opinion may be expressed with a that-clause.

originalSense.definition: A way of understanding something, an opinion, a theory.

distinctionTask.prompt: My view is that the library should stay open later. This states _____.
options: a judgement about what the hours should be
distinctionTask.answer: a judgement about what the hours should be
distinctionTask.explanation: Should identifies the proposed situation, not a factual timetable.

definition: A point of view or perspective from which something is considered.
example: In the residents’ view, the plan would improve access.
distinctions: The phrase attributes a perspective to the residents. The projected improvement has not necessarily happened.
usage: Mental noun; in someone’s view attributes a perspective.

originalSense.definition: A point of view.

distinctionTask.prompt: In the residents’ view, the plan would improve access. The improvement is presented as _____.
options: their assessment of a proposed plan
distinctionTask.answer: their assessment of a proposed plan
distinctionTask.explanation: The attributed view and would describe an assessment of the proposal.

definition: An intention, aim or prospect.
example: They are saving with a view to buying a home.
collocations: with a view to doing something
distinctions: With a view to introduces the aim of the saving. It does not establish that a purchase has occurred; to is followed by the -ing form here.
usage: Intention noun; with a view to plus an -ing form.

originalSense.definition: An intention or prospect.

distinctionTask.prompt: They save with a view to buying a home. Buying is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The construction introduces an intention.

definition: To send light or other waves back from a surface.
example: A flat mirror reflects incoming light back into the room.
distinctions: In the illustrated ideal flat-mirror case, the incident and reflected rays make equal angles to the normal. Reflection is separate from light passing through or being absorbed.
usage: Transitive: a surface reflects light; the diagram illustrates specular reflection.

originalSense.definition: To bend back (light, etc.) from a surface.
originalSense.example: A mirror reflects the light that shines on it.

distinctionTask.prompt: A flat mirror reflects a beam. The illustrated reflection sends the light _____.
options: only through the mirror without returning
distinctionTask.explanation: Reflection concerns the returning ray; transmission is a different process.

definition: Of light or similar radiation, to be sent back from a surface.
example: The light reflected from the mirror onto the wall.
distinctions: Light is the subject in this intransitive construction. In the mirror reflects light, the surface is the subject and light is its direct object.
usage: Intransitive: light reflects from or off a surface.

originalSense.definition: To be bent back (light, etc.) from a surface.
originalSense.example: The moonlight reflected from the surface of water.

distinctionTask.prompt: The light reflected from the mirror. The grammatical subject is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The intransitive construction makes the returning light the subject.

definition: To show the image of someone or something, as a mirror does.
example: The still water reflected the tree beside the pond.
distinctions: The water shows an image of the tree. The image is separate from a second physical tree, and disturbed water can produce a different appearance.
usage: Transitive: a surface reflects an object or its image.

originalSense.definition: To mirror, or show the image of something.
originalSense.example: The shop window reflected his image as he walked past.

distinctionTask.prompt: Still water reflects a tree. The reflection is _____.
options: a second living tree beneath the water
distinctionTask.explanation: An optical image does not duplicate the physical object.

definition: To appear as a mirrored image in or from a surface.
example: The tree reflected in the still water.
distinctions: The tree is the subject of this intransitive image construction. It is the image that appears in the water; the physical tree need not be in it.
usage: Intransitive; the subject appears as a mirrored image.

originalSense.definition: To be mirrored.
originalSense.example: His image reflected from the shop window as he walked past.

distinctionTask.prompt: The tree reflected in the water. This does not require _____.
options: the physical tree to be under the water
a mirrored image of the tree
distinctionTask.answer: the physical tree to be under the water
distinctionTask.explanation: The sentence concerns the tree’s image.

definition: To agree with or closely follow something.
example: The revised timetable reflects the new train times.
distinctions: The timetable is arranged to correspond to the train times. It is not a literal mirror, and reflecting a pattern need not explain what caused it.

originalSense.definition: To agree with; to closely follow.
originalSense.example: Entries in English dictionaries aim to reflect common usage.

distinctionTask.prompt: A revised timetable reflects new train times. It _____.
options: necessarily caused the trains to change
distinctionTask.explanation: Reflect here means match or closely follow, not cause.

definition: To give evidence of someone’s or something’s character or qualities.
example: Her careful preparation reflects her professionalism.
distinctions: Preparation can be evidence of professionalism. The sentence is an assessment; it does not make any one action conclusive proof of a person’s whole character.
usage: Transitive; reflect a quality. Reflect well on also evaluates how an action presents someone.

originalSense.definition: To give evidence of someone's or something's character etc.
originalSense.example: The team's victory reflects the Captain's abilities.

distinctionTask.prompt: Careful preparation reflects her professionalism. The preparation is presented as _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The context uses reflect figuratively for evidence of a quality.

definition: To think seriously about something or consider it carefully.
example: After the meeting, we reflected on what we could improve.
distinctions: Reflect on describes deliberate consideration. It does not establish that a decision was reached or an improvement completed.
usage: Intransitive; reflect on or upon a topic.

originalSense.definition: To think seriously; to ponder or consider.
originalSense.example: People do that sort of thing every day, without ever stopping to reflect on the consequences.

distinctionTask.prompt: We reflected on what we could improve. We _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Consideration is separate from completed action.

definition: To be certain that something is true or factual.
example: I know that the shop is closed today because I checked its opening hours.
distinctions: Know presents something as known to be true. Think and suppose can express an opinion or an uncertain belief; the speaker’s claim alone is not independent verification.
usage: Transitive; know a fact or know that + clause.

originalSense.definition: To perceive the truth or factuality of; to be certain of; to be certain that.
originalSense.example: Question things. I have the most fun when I'm writing questioning things that people do not question- the assumptions that everybody knows are true.

distinctionTask.prompt: I know that the shop is closed. The speaker presents the closure as _____.
options: something they know to be true
only a guess they have not accepted
distinctionTask.answer: something they know to be true
distinctionTask.explanation: Know presents knowledge, whereas I think it is closed can leave more uncertainty.

definition: To be aware or become aware, without stating a direct object.
example: The route has changed. I did not know until this morning.
distinctions: The information is supplied by the previous sentence. This intransitive use differs grammatically from I know the route, which states an object.
usage: Intransitive; the surrounding context supplies what is known.

originalSense.definition: To be or become aware or cognizant.
originalSense.example: Did you know Michelle and Jack were getting divorced? ― Yes, I knew.

distinctionTask.prompt: The route has changed. I did not know. Here the information is _____.
options: stated as a direct object after know
distinctionTask.explanation: There is no direct object after know in this example.

definition: To be aware of a fact or situation.
example: I know the risks of travelling without insurance.
distinctions: Being aware of risks does not mean approving of them or having personally experienced them. Know the risks states an object; I already know leaves the information implicit.

originalSense.definition: To be aware of; to be cognizant of.
originalSense.example: Did you know Michelle and Jack were getting divorced? ― Yes, I knew.

distinctionTask.prompt: I know the risks of travelling without insurance. I am _____.
options: necessarily willing to accept those risks
distinctionTask.explanation: Awareness alone does not establish acceptance.

definition: An obsolete intransitive use meaning to be acquainted with another person.
example: The preserved source records an obsolete intransitive acquaintance use. For present-day learning, use a direct object in I know her, or say I am acquainted with her.
distinctions: The obsolete label concerns this intransitive record. It does not apply to the everyday transitive I know her.

originalSense.definition: To be acquainted (with another person).
originalSense.example: You, and I haue knowne ſir.

definition: To be acquainted or familiar with a person, place or thing.
example: I know our new neighbour; we met last year.
distinctions: Know a person describes familiarity. Meet describes an encounter; knowing someone does not mean knowing every fact about them.
usage: Transitive; know + person, place or thing.

originalSense.definition: To be acquainted or familiar with; to have encountered.
originalSense.example: I know your mother, but I've never met your father.

distinctionTask.prompt: I know our new neighbour; we met last year. Know expresses _____.
options: only a plan to meet them for the first time
distinctionTask.explanation: The sentence states an existing acquaintance.

definition: To experience a condition, feeling or event.
example: The town has known severe flooding in the past.
distinctions: The town has experienced flooding. This literary or formal use differs from residents merely knowing information about a flood.
usage: Transitive; often with an experience or condition.

originalSense.definition: To experience.
originalSense.example: Their relationship knew ups and downs.

distinctionTask.prompt: The town has known severe flooding. This says the town _____.
options: only holds information about floods elsewhere
distinctionTask.explanation: Know here describes experience.

definition: To understand a subject or know how to do something through study or experience.
example: She knows how to repair a puncture because she has practised.
distinctions: Know how to concerns practical or explanatory knowledge. Know that a tyre is flat states a fact and does not by itself establish repair skill.
usage: Know how to + verb; know how + clause; know a subject.

originalSense.definition: To understand or have a grasp of through experience or study.
originalSense.example: Let me do it. I know how it works.

distinctionTask.prompt: She knows how to repair a puncture. This concerns _____.
options: knowledge of how to carry out the repair
only awareness that a puncture exists
distinctionTask.answer: knowledge of how to carry out the repair
distinctionTask.explanation: Know how to describes procedural knowledge.

definition: To distinguish one thing from another or recognise its nature.
example: She knows right from wrong.
distinctions: Know A from B concerns discrimination between things. Recognising that a familiar person has returned is a separate recognition use.
usage: Transitive; especially know A from B.

originalSense.definition: To be able to distinguish, to discern, particularly by contrast or comparison; to recognize the nature of.
originalSense.example: to know a person's face or figure

distinctionTask.prompt: She knows right from wrong. She can _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The construction know A from B expresses discrimination.

definition: To recognise someone or something encountered before, despite an absence or change.
example: Even after twenty years, I knew her at once by her voice.
distinctions: The speaker recognises the same person again. Familiarity enables this recognition; the sentence does not say they first met at that moment.
usage: Transitive; knew is the past tense of know.

originalSense.definition: To recognize as the same (as someone or something previously encountered) after an absence or change.
originalSense.example: At nearer view he thought he knew the dead, / And call'd the wretched man to mind.

distinctionTask.prompt: After twenty years, I knew her at once by her voice. I _____.
options: recognised someone I had met before
met her for the first time
distinctionTask.answer: recognised someone I had met before
distinctionTask.explanation: The voice prompts renewed recognition.

definition: To possess knowledge or information, without specifying a direct object.
example: Ask the receptionist; she will know.
distinctions: Will know here means will have the relevant information. It does not describe a future first meeting with a person.
usage: Intransitive; context supplies the relevant information.

originalSense.definition: To have knowledge; to have information, be informed.
originalSense.example: It is vital that he not know.

distinctionTask.prompt: Ask the receptionist; she will know. She is expected to _____.
options: introduce herself for the first time
distinctionTask.explanation: No direct object is stated; the question supplies the topic.

definition: To be able to play, sing or otherwise perform a piece of music.
example: The pianist knows the opening song and can play it from memory.
distinctions: Here knows concerns ability to perform the piece. Know of a song can mean only having heard that it exists.
usage: Transitive; know a song, tune or piece.

originalSense.definition: To be able to play or perform (a song or other piece of music).
originalSense.example: Do you know "Blueberry Hill"?

distinctionTask.prompt: The pianist knows the song and can play it from memory. Know here concerns _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The explicit ability to play identifies the musical meaning.

definition: Of a database or system, to have indexed information about something.
example: The catalogue knows this title because the record is in its database.
distinctions: This personifies a system’s stored or indexed information. It does not imply human awareness or that the record’s contents are correct.
usage: Technical, transitive use; the subject can be a system.

originalSense.definition: To have indexed and have information about within one's database.
originalSense.example: Mmm... Seems you searched for a name that we don't know, we'll send our trained monkeys to check what's in stock.

distinctionTask.prompt: The catalogue knows this title because it has an indexed record. This establishes _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Know is a technical personification of indexed information.

definition: In philosophy, to have knowledge according to the account of knowledge being discussed.
example: A philosophical discussion may ask whether a person who holds a justified true belief knows it. Gettier-style objections show why justified true belief is not universally accepted as sufficient for knowledge.
distinctions: Justified true belief is one traditional account of knowledge. Gettier-style objections challenge its sufficiency, so it should not be presented as an uncontested definition.
usage: Philosophical sense; the relevant criteria depend on the account under discussion.

originalSense.definition: To maintain (a belief, a position) subject to a given philosophical definition of knowledge; to hold a justified true belief.

definition: A rare noun meaning knowledge or the state of knowing.
example: In the source’s Hamlet quotation, know is a noun for knowledge or awareness of the contents. In ordinary present-day prose, knowledge is the usual independent noun.
distinctions: This rare independent noun differs from the familiar fixed phrase in the know. Its literary attestation does not make ordinary verb know obsolete.
usage: Rare noun; reading guidance for the preserved literary source.

originalSense.definition: Knowledge; the state of knowing.
originalSense.example: That on the view and know of theſe Contents, […] He ſhould the bearers put to […] death, […]

definition: Knowledge of a matter, now used in the fixed phrase in the know.
example: Staff in the know told us that the opening date had changed.
distinctions: In the know means informed about a matter, often information unavailable to others. It does not mean physically located inside a place.
usage: Noun within the fixed phrase in the know.

originalSense.definition: Knowledge; the state of knowing. (Now confined to the fixed phrase in the know.)

distinctionTask.prompt: Staff in the know told us the new opening date. They were _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The fixed phrase describes access to information.

definition: An alternative noun form of knowe, meaning a hill or knoll.
example: The preserved quotation names Fox’s Know while discussing a place where birds nest. Here Know belongs to the hill or knoll noun, independently of the verb meaning have knowledge.
collocations: know as a form of knowe
distinctions: This is an alternative noun form of knowe, not an accidental spelling error. In the know means informed and is unrelated to a hill.
usage: Alternative form of knowe; a separate noun etymology.

originalSense.definition: Alternative form of knowe (“hill, knoll”).
originalSense.example: Owing to increasing numbers and consequent want of room for nestage, the old birds drove away the younger ones, who took refuge in their present abode at Fox's Know, where they have been located about six years.

definition: In Singlish, a sentence-final particle drawing attention to information the listener should keep in mind.
example: The source gives Make sure you water the plants, know… . The final know draws the listener’s attention; it is not a request to define the word plants.
distinctions: This is a regional discourse particle, not the ordinary verb with a missing object. The source says not to combine it with other sentence-final discourse particles.
usage: Singlish particle; regional conversational usage, with source-specific reading guidance.

originalSense.definition: Used at the end of a sentence to draw attention to information one thinks the listener should keep in mind.
originalSense.example: Make sure you water the plants, know…

definition: An archaic, Biblical or euphemistic use meaning to have sexual relations with someone.
example: In older Biblical language, know someone can mean have sexual relations with them. Modern explanations often specify know in the biblical sense to make this euphemistic meaning clear.
distinctions: This labelled historical meaning is distinct from ordinary acquaintance. Knowing a neighbour in the everyday sense implies no sexual relationship.
usage: Archaic, Biblical and euphemistic; reading guidance.

originalSense.definition: To have sexual relations with. This meaning normally specified in modern English as e.g. to 'know someone in the biblical sense' or to 'know biblically'.

definition: In Singlish, a discourse marker equivalent to you know, used to emphasise something.
example: In Singlish conversation, this know works like you know as a discourse marker. It can add emphasis or help manage a turn, rather than assert that the listener knows a particular fact.
collocations: you know as a discourse marker
distinctions: This regional conversational use adds emphasis or helps manage a turn. Ordinary know that instead introduces information presented as known.

originalSense.definition: Synonym of you know (used as a conversational discourse marker, to emphasize something).

definition: To comprehend the meaning of words, statements, signs or other communication.
example: I understand the instructions, so I can explain what they ask us to do.
distinctions: Understanding a message concerns its meaning. Hearing its sounds or reading its words does not by itself establish comprehension or agreement.
usage: Transitive or intransitive; communication is the focus of this source record.

originalSense.definition: To know the meaning of; to parse or have parsed correctly; to comprehend.
originalSense.example: Can you repeat what you just said? I didn't understand.
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: I understand the instructions. This means I _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Comprehension is separate from agreement.

definition: To be familiar enough with a skill, task or profession to carry it out properly.
example: She understands her job and can organise the work without help.
distinctions: This concerns practical familiarity with a task. Knowing a job title alone does not establish competence to do the work.
usage: Transitive; the object is a skill, task or profession.

originalSense.definition: To be thoroughly familiar with; to be able to undertake properly.
originalSense.example: The students understood the assignment.
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: She understands her job and can organise the work. This concerns _____.
options: only recognition of her job title
distinctionTask.explanation: The stated ability identifies familiarity with the task.

definition: To comprehend a fact or principle, or come to regard a belief as one.
example: The pupils understand that water expands when it freezes.
distinctions: The clause states what is comprehended. The source also includes coming to regard a belief as fact; the verb alone cannot independently verify every proposition introduced by that.

originalSense.definition: To comprehend a fact or principle; to regard or come to regard a belief as such.
originalSense.example: I understand that company policy says I can't get a refund, but can you make an exception?
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: The pupils understand that water expands when it freezes. The clause states _____.
options: the words omitted from an imperative
distinctionTask.explanation: This is conceptual comprehension, not grammatical ellipsis.

definition: To comprehend a person’s motives or character, or the reasons for an event.
example: I understand why she left early: she had to collect her child.
distinctions: Understanding why someone acted does not necessarily mean approving of the action. With events, the focus is their causes or reasons.
usage: Transitive; people, motives and reasons for events.

originalSense.definition: To know the intent, motives or character of; (of events) to know the causes of or reasons for.
originalSense.example: One day you say you love me, the next you ignore me—I don't understand you!
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: I understand why she left early. This does not necessarily mean I _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Comprehension of a motive and approval are separate judgements.

definition: To believe or infer something on the basis of information that may be incomplete.
example: I understand that the meeting has moved to Friday, but I have not checked.
distinctions: I understand that can report an inference or received information. Here the speaker explicitly has not checked; this is not independent confirmation of Friday.
usage: Transitive; often a cautious report of one’s present understanding.

originalSense.definition: To believe or infer, to think one grasps sufficiently despite potentially incomplete knowledge.
originalSense.example: I've been given to understand that you have a package for me?

distinctionTask.prompt: I understand the meeting is on Friday, but I have not checked. Friday is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The explicit qualification leaves the information unverified.

definition: In grammar, to interpret an unexpressed word or element as implicit.
example: In the command Sit down, you is understood as the subject.
distinctions: An understood subject is implicit in the grammatical interpretation. It is not printed in the command, and this technical use does not mean that a listener agrees to obey.
usage: Grammatical sense; often passive, as in the subject is understood.

originalSense.definition: To regard as present when not.
originalSense.example: In the imperative mood, the word “you” is usually understood.
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: In Sit down, the subject you is understood. It is _____.
options: a visible word in the command
distinctionTask.explanation: The command has no written you, but the subject is interpreted.

definition: A rare literal use meaning to stand underneath and support, especially in acrobatics.
example: The checked source labels literal understand humorous and rare, and obsolete except in circus acrobatics. It describes standing beneath and supporting another performer, rather than comprehending an idea.
distinctions: The circus exception belongs to this rare literal record. It does not make the everyday comprehension verb obsolete.
usage: Humorous and rare; obsolete except in circus acrobatics, according to the checked source.

originalSense.definition: To stand underneath, to support.
originalSense.example:
LAUNE: Ay, and what I do too: look thee, I'll but lean, and my staff understands me.
SPEED: It stands under thee, indeed.
LAUNCE:Why, stand-under and under-stand is all one.
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

definition: In Singapore and Malaysia, an interjection acknowledging what another speaker has said.
example: The checked source records understand as a backchannel, comparable to uh-huh or I see. In this use a listener acknowledges a turn in conversation; it is not automatically a command to someone else.
distinctions: This regional interjection is distinct from the imperative Understand! and the question Do you understand? Acknowledgement also need not imply agreement.

originalSense.definition: Uh-huh, I see; a way to acknowledge something said by the other speaker.

definition: To know the meaning of something.
example: Do you understand the meaning of this symbol?
distinctions: Understanding a symbol means interpreting what it signifies. Recognising its shape or colour alone does not show that its meaning is understood.
usage: Transitive; understand the meaning of + noun phrase.

originalSense.definition: To know the meaning of.

distinctionTask.prompt: To understand the meaning of a symbol is to know _____.
options: only the colour of the page
distinctionTask.explanation: Meaning concerns what the symbol signifies.

definition: To take or keep hold of something, especially with the hand.
example: She grasped the handrail firmly as the boat moved.
distinctions: This is physical holding. Grasp an explanation instead concerns understanding, and grasp at something can describe an attempt without a secure hold.

originalSense.definition: To grip; to take hold, particularly with the hand.
originalSense.example: How few! yet how they creep / Through my fingers to the deep, / While I weep—while I weep! / O God! can I not grasp / Them with a tighter clasp?
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

distinctionTask.prompt: She grasped the handrail firmly. She _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The handrail and physical action identify the literal meaning.

definition: To understand an idea, explanation or situation.
example: After seeing the diagram, he grasped how the pump worked.
distinctions: Grasp emphasises getting an intellectual hold of something. Knowing that a pump exists does not establish understanding of how it works.
usage: Verb; grasp an idea or grasp how/that + clause.

originalSense.definition: To understand.
originalSense.example: I have never been able to grasp the concept of infinity.
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

distinctionTask.prompt: He grasped how the pump worked. This means he _____.
options: held the pump in his hand by definition
distinctionTask.explanation: The how clause identifies intellectual comprehension.

definition: To seize or take advantage of an opportunity.
example: She grasped the opportunity to study abroad and applied that evening.
distinctions: The opportunity is acted on, not physically held. Taking the chance does not by itself guarantee admission or a successful outcome.
usage: Verb; figurative grasp + opportunity or chance.

originalSense.definition: To take advantage of something, to seize, to jump at a chance.
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

distinctionTask.prompt: She grasped the opportunity and applied. The sentence establishes _____.
options: that she acted on the opportunity
that she was admitted to the course
distinctionTask.answer: that she acted on the opportunity
distinctionTask.explanation: Seizing an opportunity and obtaining a successful result are separate.

definition: A firm hold or grip, sometimes used figuratively for control.
example: The rope slipped from his grasp.
distinctions: This noun names the hold itself. A grasp of the method instead concerns understanding; grasp can also figuratively describe control.
usage: Noun; literal grip or figurative control.

originalSense.definition: Grip.
originalSense.example: A vagrant gust of wind snatched the note from my grasp.
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

distinctionTask.prompt: The rope slipped from his grasp. Grasp names _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The object slipping identifies a physical grip.

definition: An understanding of a subject or situation.
example: She has a good grasp of basic statistics and can explain the results.
collocations: a firm grasp of a subject
distinctions: A grasp of statistics is knowledge or understanding, not a physical grip. Good modifies grasp; a grasp on can also occur, but of is the construction in this example.

originalSense.definition: Understanding.
originalSense.example: There is for the mind but one grasp of happiness: from that uppermost pinnacle of wisdom, whence we see that this world is well designed.
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

distinctionTask.prompt: She has a good grasp of basic statistics. This concerns _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The subject after of identifies intellectual understanding.

definition: The range of what someone can reach, obtain or achieve.
example: The top shelf is beyond the child’s grasp.
distinctions: Beyond the child’s grasp means beyond reach here. The same range expression can refer figuratively to attainability; it does not always mean failure to understand.
usage: Noun; often within or beyond someone’s grasp.

originalSense.definition: That which is accessible; that which is within one's reach or ability.
originalSense.example: The goal is within my grasp.
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

distinctionTask.prompt: The top shelf is beyond the child’s grasp. Here the shelf is _____.
options: too difficult for the child to understand
distinctionTask.explanation: The physical shelf identifies reach rather than comprehension.

definition: GRASP: General Responsibility Assignment Software Patterns or Principles, used in object-oriented design.
example: In software design, GRASP names principles for assigning responsibilities to objects. Information Expert and Low Coupling are examples; the uppercase acronym is distinct from the ordinary verb grasp.
distinctions: This is the software acronym from the capitalised GRASP source page. It is independent of the separate anti-spam team acronym.
usage: Capitalised software acronym; source page GRASP.

originalSense.definition: Acronym of General Responsibility Assignment Software Patterns (or Principles).
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

definition: GRASP: Gamepedia Rapid Anti-Spam Patrol, the name of an anti-spam team.
example: The checked capitalised source records Gamepedia Rapid Anti-Spam Patrol as a team name abbreviated GRASP. The record identifies that name; it does not establish the team’s current status or activity.
distinctions: The team acronym and the software-design acronym share spelling but have different referents. Neither should replace the ordinary comprehension meaning.
usage: Capitalised proper name; source page GRASP.

originalSense.definition: Acronym of Gamepedia Rapid Anti-Spam Patrol.
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

definition: To feel grateful or thankful for something.
example: I appreciate your help with the application.
distinctions: Appreciate your help takes the thing appreciated as its direct object. Say thank you for your help or I am grateful to you; appreciate is not normally followed directly by a person meaning thank that person.
usage: Transitive; appreciate + noun phrase or -ing form.

originalSense.definition: To be grateful or thankful for.
originalSense.example: I appreciate your efforts.

distinctionTask.prompt: I appreciate your help with the application. I am expressing _____.
options: a rise in the application’s price
distinctionTask.explanation: The object your help identifies gratitude.

definition: To recognise and value the worth or qualities of something.
example: She appreciates the craftsmanship of the handmade bowl.
distinctions: Valuing craftsmanship does not require thanking the bowl or buying it. Appreciate a risk instead means recognise or understand it, not approve of it.
usage: Transitive; value or recognise the qualities of an object, activity or person.

originalSense.definition: To view as valuable.
originalSense.example: You must learn to appreciate time.

distinctionTask.prompt: She appreciates the bowl’s craftsmanship. This means she _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Appreciation of quality does not establish a purchase.

definition: To fully recognise, understand or become conscious of something.
example: We appreciate the risks involved and will review the safety plan.
distinctions: Recognising a risk does not mean enjoying it, approving of it or being grateful for it. The source’s broad awareness record can also include detecting a feature.
usage: Transitive; often the difficulty, extent, importance or risk of something.

originalSense.definition: To be fully conscious of; understand; be aware of; detect.
originalSense.example: Near-synonyms: realize, grasp, acknowledge

distinctionTask.prompt: We appreciate the risks involved. Here appreciate means _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Awareness is distinct from gratitude or approval.

definition: To increase in value, or cause something to increase in value.
example: The painting appreciated from £1,000 to £1,200 over five years.
distinctions: Here the painting’s value rises; no person is expressing thanks. The source also records a transitive increase-in-value use. A rise over one period does not promise future gains or an inflation-adjusted profit.
usage: Usually intransitive in this example; the source also records transitive use.

originalSense.definition: To increase in value.
originalSense.example: The value of his portfolio appreciated by 80% over eight years.

distinctionTask.prompt: The painting appreciated from £1,000 to £1,200. Its value _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Appreciate in value is the opposite direction from depreciate.

definition: To predict or believe that something will happen.
example: I expect rain tomorrow, although I hope it stays dry.
distinctions: Expect reports a prediction here; hope expresses a desired outcome. A prediction can concern something unwanted and does not guarantee that it will happen.
usage: With a noun, a that-clause or a to-infinitive; the source also records use without an expressed object.

originalSense.definition: To predict or believe that something will happen
originalSense.example: when you least expect it

distinctionTask.prompt: I expect rain tomorrow, although I hope it stays dry. The speaker _____.
options: predicts rain but would prefer dry weather
knows with certainty that rain will fall
distinctionTask.answer: predicts rain but would prefer dry weather
distinctionTask.explanation: Expect expresses a belief about the future; hope identifies the preferred outcome.

definition: To consider something obligatory or required.
example: The course rules are clear: we expect every student to submit work on time.
distinctions: The rules make this a requirement. Expect can also express a prediction, so the surrounding context determines the sense; requiring punctuality does not prove that everyone is punctual.
usage: Often expect + person + to-infinitive; a requirement can also appear in a that-clause.

originalSense.definition: To consider obligatory or required.
originalSense.example: England expects that every man will do his duty.

distinctionTask.prompt: The course rules say we expect every student to submit work on time. This states _____.
options: proof that all work has already been submitted
distinctionTask.explanation: Rules establish what is required, not whether it has been done.

definition: To regard something as reasonably due or deserved.
example: As paying customers, we expect a reasonable standard of service.
distinctions: The customers regard decent service as reasonably due. This overlaps with prediction in some contexts but does not establish a legal entitlement or guarantee that the service will meet the standard.
usage: Expect something of or from someone can concern the standard reasonably asked of them.

originalSense.definition: To consider reasonably due.
originalSense.example: My parents expected too much of me when I was in college.

distinctionTask.prompt: As paying customers, we expect a reasonable standard of service. The customers _____.
options: regard decent service as reasonably due
confirm that the service has already been excellent
distinctionTask.answer: regard decent service as reasonably due
distinctionTask.explanation: The statement expresses an expected standard, not an observed service result.

definition: In the continuous aspect, to be pregnant or to have a baby due as a couple.
example: We are expecting a baby in June.
distinctions: We are expecting can be said by a couple. It does not mean that every person included in we is pregnant, and a due month is not a guaranteed birth date.
usage: Use the continuous construction be expecting in this meaning.

originalSense.definition: To be pregnant, to consider a baby due.
originalSense.example: We are expecting our third in June.

distinctionTask.prompt: A couple say, “We are expecting a baby in June.” This means _____.
options: they have a baby due in June
distinctionTask.answer: they have a baby due in June
distinctionTask.explanation: A couple can use we are expecting; the plural subject does not assign pregnancy to each partner.

definition: Obsolete: to wait for or await someone or something.
example: Reading note: in Shakespeare’s “there expect their coming”, expect means wait for their arrival. The quoted construction takes their coming as its object.
distinctions: This source-labelled obsolete wait-for sense is separate from modern expect meaning predict. The quotation is explained for reading rather than presented as a new everyday sentence.
usage: Obsolete, transitive in the checked source.

originalSense.definition: To wait for; to await.
originalSense.example: Let's in, and there expect their coming.

definition: Obsolete: to wait or stay.
example: Reading note: the source’s “I will expect until my change in death” uses expect for waiting, with an until-clause and no direct object.
collocations: expect without an object (obsolete wait sense)
distinctions: This obsolete intransitive wait sense differs from the obsolete transitive await construction and from a modern prediction. The source line is interpreted rather than offered as an everyday model.
usage: Obsolete, intransitive in the checked source.

originalSense.definition: To wait; to stay.
originalSense.example: I will 'expect until my change in death, / And answer at Thy call

definition: To act before someone, especially to prevent or forestall their action.
example: To anticipate the critic, the speaker answers the objection before it is raised.
distinctions: Here the speaker acts before the critic raises an objection. Merely expecting criticism does not by itself mean taking preventive action, and an early answer need not stop every later criticism.
usage: Transitive; this meaning concerns acting before someone.

originalSense.definition: To act before (someone), especially to prevent an action.
originalSense.example:
c. 1824 (written, published in 1891) Robert Hall, Fragment on Popery
When two parties, each formidable for their numbers, and the weight of their influence and property, are animated by an equal degree of zeal, it is natural to anticipate the final success of that which possesses the most inherent strength.

distinctionTask.prompt: To anticipate the critic, the speaker answers an objection before it is raised. The speaker _____.
options: acts before the critic raises it
waits until after the critic has raised it
distinctionTask.answer: acts before the critic raises it
distinctionTask.explanation: The before-clause explicitly places the answer ahead of the objection.

definition: To take up or introduce something prematurely or ahead of its proper place.
example: Let me anticipate the next chapter by discussing its conclusion now.
distinctions: This introduces material earlier than its planned place. It is distinct from merely predicting what the chapter will say; the checked source does not label this meaning obsolete.
usage: Transitive; a topic, argument or later part of an account is introduced ahead of its place.

originalSense.definition: To take up or introduce (something) prematurely.
originalSense.example: The advocate plans to anticipate a part of her argument.

distinctionTask.prompt: Let me anticipate the next chapter by discussing its conclusion now. This proposes _____.
options: introducing later material ahead of its place
postponing all discussion of the conclusion
distinctionTask.answer: introducing later material ahead of its place
distinctionTask.explanation: Now and next chapter establish that the material is being brought forward.

definition: To foresee or expect something before it happens.
example: We anticipate delays because repairs are planned on the line.
distinctions: Anticipate and expect overlap in this predictive sense. Anticipating delays need not mean looking forward to them, and planned repairs do not guarantee a particular delay.
usage: Transitive; followed by a noun, an -ing form or a clause.

originalSense.definition: To know of (something) before it happens; to expect.
originalSense.example: to anticipate the pleasures of a visit

distinctionTask.prompt: We anticipate delays because repairs are planned. Here anticipate means _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A forecast can concern an unwanted event; eager pleasure is not required.

definition: To wait eagerly for something.
example: The children eagerly anticipate their visit to the aquarium.
distinctions: Eagerly and the visit context identify looking forward to an event. Anticipate elsewhere can simply mean expect, including expecting something unpleasant.
usage: Transitive; an event or arrival is eagerly awaited.

originalSense.definition: To eagerly wait for (something)
originalSense.example: Little Johnny started to anticipate the arrival of Santa Claus a week before Christmas.

distinctionTask.prompt: The children eagerly anticipate their aquarium visit. They _____.
options: have necessarily completed the visit already
distinctionTask.explanation: Eager anticipation concerns a visit still ahead, not a completed experience.

definition: To believe or conclude something without absolute supporting evidence.
example: I suppose the office is closed, but I have not checked.
distinctions: I suppose marks a belief that may be uncertain. Assume and presume can overlap with it; there is no universal fixed evidence threshold separating these words.
usage: Can take a clause or be used with an understood proposition, as in I suppose so.

originalSense.definition: To take for granted; to conclude, with less than absolute supporting data; to believe.
originalSense.example: I suppose we all agree that this is the best solution.

distinctionTask.prompt: I suppose the office is closed, but I have not checked. The speaker _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The explicit lack of checking rules out a claim of verification.

definition: To put forward a theory or hypothesis for consideration.
example: Suppose x = 4; then 2x = 8.
distinctions: The value x = 4 is a premise for this calculation. The implication does not establish that x has that value in an actual measurement.
usage: Often imperative suppose introduces a hypothetical premise.

originalSense.definition: To theorize or hypothesize.
originalSense.example: Suppose that A implies B and B implies C. Then A implies C.

distinctionTask.prompt: Suppose x = 4; then 2x = 8. The calculation _____.
options: proves that every possible x equals 4
distinctionTask.explanation: The result is conditional on the stated value, not a proof of that value in every case.

definition: To imagine, believe or accept something as true.
example: Do not suppose that every expensive course is a good one.
distinctions: This warns against accepting price as a guarantee of quality. The source meaning overlaps with uncertain belief; the warning neither proves that all expensive courses are good nor that all are bad.
usage: Transitive; can introduce the proposition someone imagines or accepts.

originalSense.definition: To imagine; to believe; to receive as true.
originalSense.example: How easy is a bush supposed a bear!

distinctionTask.prompt: Do not suppose that every expensive course is good. This warns against _____.
options: accepting price alone as a guarantee of quality
believing that any expensive course can ever be good
distinctionTask.answer: accepting price alone as a guarantee of quality
distinctionTask.explanation: Rejecting the blanket assumption does not establish the opposite blanket claim.

definition: Obsolete: to reckon, account or esteem someone or something as a particular thing.
example: Reading note: in the source’s “Being supposed his worthless Concubine”, supposed means regarded or accounted as. The social description belongs to the quotation.
distinctions: This source-labelled obsolete estimation use is separate from modern be supposed to expressing an expectation or obligation. The quotation’s description is not an editorial judgment about a person.
usage: Obsolete, transitive in the checked source.

originalSense.definition: To reckon to be, to account or esteem as.
originalSense.example:
[He] keeps you from the honors of a Queene,
Being ſuppoſde his worthleſſe Concubine.

definition: To require something to exist or be true; to presuppose it.
example: Such arguments suppose that everyone has internet access.
distinctions: The argument relies on access as a premise. This does not prove that everyone actually has access, nor does it mean the argument orders someone to obtain it.
usage: Transitive; often formal, with an argument or proposition as subject.

originalSense.definition: To require to exist or to be true; to imply by the laws of thought or of nature.
originalSense.example: Purpose supposes foresight.

distinctionTask.prompt: Such arguments suppose that everyone has internet access. Internet access is _____.
options: a premise on which the arguments rely
proved universal by the word suppose
distinctionTask.answer: a premise on which the arguments rely
distinctionTask.explanation: Presupposing a condition does not independently establish its truth.

definition: Obsolete: to put something in another’s place by fraud; to substitute fraudulently.
example: Reading note: the checked source uses supposeth in an account of a changeling belief, meaning substitutes another child in place of the first. This explains the story’s wording, not evidence that such a substitution occurred.
collocations: suppose another in its place (source construction)
distinctions: This obsolete fraudulent-substitution sense is different from forming a belief. The supernatural account is a reported belief and must not be treated as a confirmed event.
usage: Obsolete, transitive in the checked source.

originalSense.definition: To put by fraud in the place of another; to substitute fraudulently.
originalSense.example: A Water-monster, called the Nickard, does enter by night the chamber, where a woman is brought to bed, and stealeth when they are all sleeping, the new-born child and supposeth another in its place, which child growing up is like a monster and commonly dumb.

definition: A desire, hope or longing for something or for something to happen.
example: She has a strong wish to study abroad.
distinctions: The noun describes a desire. Having that desire does not establish a plan, admission or completed study; wish and hope overlap rather than following an absolute possible/impossible rule.
usage: Countable noun; wish to + infinitive or wish for + noun can identify the desire.

originalSense.definition: A desire, hope, or longing for something or for something to happen.
originalSense.example: It is my wish that the bequest (should) be given to an almshouse.

distinctionTask.prompt: She has a strong wish to study abroad. This states _____.
options: proof that she has been admitted abroad
distinctionTask.explanation: A wish alone does not establish admission or completion.

definition: An expression of a desire, often associated with ideas of magic or supernatural power.
example: Make a wish before you blow out the birthday candles.
distinctions: Make a wish refers to expressing or forming the wish in this custom. The custom does not establish that magic works or that the desired result will happen.
usage: Countable noun; commonly in make a wish.

originalSense.definition: An expression of such a desire, often connected with ideas of magic and supernatural power.
originalSense.example: make a wish

distinctionTask.prompt: Make a wish before blowing out the birthday candles. This asks for _____.
options: proof that the desire will come true
distinctionTask.explanation: A customary wish expresses a desire without guaranteeing its fulfilment.

definition: The thing or outcome that someone desires or longs for.
example: Her dearest wish is a home near the sea.
distinctions: Here a home near the sea identifies the desired thing. Naming the wish does not establish ownership or a completed move; the noun can focus on the desire itself or its object in overlapping contexts.
usage: Countable noun; a following complement can identify the desired thing or outcome.

originalSense.definition: The thing desired or longed for.
originalSense.example: My dearest wish is to see them happily married.

distinctionTask.prompt: Her dearest wish is a home near the sea. What is the desired thing? _____
distinctionTask.explanation: The sentence identifies what she wants, not a purchase already made.

definition: In Sussex usage, a water meadow.
example: Reading note: the checked source labels wish meaning water meadow as Sussex usage. This is a regional landscape noun, independent of the desire noun and its verbs.
distinctions: The preserved import omits the Sussex label; the checked revision supplies it. Regional does not by itself mean obsolete, and this note does not claim the word is ordinary general English for a meadow.
usage: Sussex regional noun in the checked source.

originalSense.definition: A water meadow.

definition: To desire or want something.
example: We can change the date if you wish it.
distinctions: Here it refers to changing the date; the object can also be understood in if you wish. Wish for + noun and wish to + infinitive have separate source records but share the idea of desire.
usage: Transitive; an object may be understood from context.

originalSense.definition: To desire; to want.
originalSense.example: I'll come tomorrow, if you wish (it).

distinctionTask.prompt: We can change the date if you wish it. Here it refers to _____.
options: proof that the date has already changed
distinctionTask.explanation: Wish expresses the person’s preference; it does not report that a change has occurred.

definition: Now rare: to hope, with an object clause containing may or a present subjunctive.
example: Reading note: in Jane Austen’s “I wish it may be so”, wish means hope. The preserved import says archaic; the checked source revision labels this construction now rare.
collocations: wish it may be so (source quotation)
distinctions: The source records a rare hope construction. Rare and archaic are different labels, and this quotation does not make every use of wish with a clause archaic.
usage: Now rare in the checked revision; imported label: archaic.

originalSense.definition: To hope (+ object clause with may or in present subjunctive).
originalSense.example: I wish he mean me well, that he takes so much pains!

definition: To hope for or desire a particular outcome, even one that is unlikely or impossible.
example: We wish for a peaceful end to the dispute.
distinctions: Wish for takes a noun phrase. The desired outcome may be possible, unlikely or impossible; the construction does not by itself predict success. Modern hope for can overlap with it.
usage: Usually wish for + noun phrase in this meaning; wishes can also be expressed with clauses.

originalSense.definition: To hope (for a particular outcome), even if that outcome is unlikely to occur or cannot occur.
originalSense.example: This is as good an argument as an antiquary could wish for.

distinctionTask.prompt: We wish for a peaceful end to the dispute. This expresses _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A wish for an outcome does not guarantee it.

definition: To direct a thought, greeting or gesture towards someone or something.
example: We wish you every success in your new job.
distinctions: Wish someone success expresses goodwill. It neither promises to supply the success nor reports an achieved result; the source also records ill wishes.
usage: Ditransitive: wish + recipient + wished thing; also wish something on someone.

originalSense.definition: To bestow (a thought or gesture) towards (someone or something).

originalSense.definition: To break to pieces; to shatter.

usage: Labelled obsolete and colloquial in the checked source. Reading explanation rather than a current example.

definition: To drive away, disperse or shake something off.

definition: An argument or disagreement between people or groups.

distinctionTask.prompt: A dispute arose over the shared fence. This reports _____.

definition: Verbal controversy or disagreement considered as an activity or condition.

originalSense.definition: Verbal controversy or disagreement; altercation; debate.

distinctionTask.prompt: There was much dispute about the interpretation. Dispute is used _____.

definition: To argue against a view or claim maintained by someone else.
example: The researchers continued to dispute with one another over the interpretation.

originalSense.definition: To contend in argument; to argue against something maintained, upheld, or claimed, by another.
originalSense.example: "Now, though thy thoughts are green and tender, as becometh one so young, yet are they those of a thinking brain, and in truth thou dost bring back to my mind certain of those old philosophers with whom in days bygone I have disputed at Athens, and at Becca in Arabia, for thou hast the same crabbed air and dusty look, as though thou hadst passed thy days in reading ill-writ Greek, and been stained dark with the grime of manuscripts."

distinctionTask.prompt: The researchers continued to dispute with one another. The example _____.
options: describes arguing without a direct-object claim
proves that one researcher is correct

distinctionTask.explanation: This is the intransitive arguing construction; it supplies no independent verdict.

definition: To examine a question by arguing for and against it.
example: At the seminar, they will dispute the question, weighing arguments for and against it.
distinctions: The intended activity examines arguments on both sides. The example does not assert that everyone denied the same proposition.
usage: Retained transitive debating sense. Discuss and debate may also fit some such contexts; they are not universally wrong substitutes.

originalSense.definition: To make a subject of disputation; to argue pro and con; to discuss.

distinctionTask.prompt: They will dispute the question, weighing arguments for and against it. The intended activity is _____.

distinctionTask.explanation: The explicit for-and-against context identifies the debating meaning.

definition: To challenge the truth, validity or correctness of something.
example: The tenant will dispute the charge because she says the repair was never made.

originalSense.definition: To oppose by argument or assertion; to controvert; to express dissent or opposition to; to call into question; to deny the truth or validity of.

distinctionTask.prompt: The tenant will dispute the charge. This means _____.
options: its invalidity has already been proved
distinctionTask.explanation: A challenge is a position or action, not proof of its merits.

definition: To compete or contend for possession or control of something.
example: The two countries dispute control of the island.

usage: Transitive contest sense. The competing claims do not establish a settled outcome.

originalSense.definition: To strive or contend about; to contest.

distinctionTask.prompt: Two countries dispute control of an island. The sentence _____.

definition: To struggle against or resist something.

usage: Obsolete in the checked source; retained as a reading explanation.

originalSense.definition: To struggle against; to resist.

definition: A disagreement between parties in a contract, lawsuit, treaty or other legal matter.

originalSense.definition: A disagreement between parties in a contract, lawsuit, treaty, or other legal matter.

distinctionTask.prompt: A contract dispute has been referred to mediation. The sentence _____.

guarantees that a settlement has been reached

definition: To take part in an argument or exchange of opposing views, especially in public.

usage: Verb used transitively or intransitively. Discuss and debate can overlap; public opposing viewpoints are explicit in this example.

originalSense.definition: To participate in a debate; to dispute, argue, especially in a public arena.

distinctionTask.prompt: The candidates will debate transport policy on Friday. This reports _____.

a final decision already accepted by both

definition: To fight or engage in combat.
example: The source records an obsolete intransitive combat sense of debate. It concerns fighting, rather than a modern public exchange of arguments.

originalSense.definition: To fight.
